You’ve crystallized that belief and made it part of you, and thus, that’s how you will act. That makes change so much harder. If you really are lazy, the “I am” statement has boxed you in that corner and branded itself to you.
The original rule, which was formed in the context of economics, stated that in any given endeavor, 80% of consequences stem from 20% of the causes.

So, in your planning, learn about the most universal and commonly studied aspects first. If you’re learning US History, you’ll focus on major events that shaped the landscape: wars, economics, civil rights, political leaders, maybe a few others. Sure, you could study major sports events, the popularity of action figures, and the fishing industry—but right at first? No. They’re of peripheral importance at best. When you understand the general landscape of economics and warfare, you can probably guess how each element flows from them.

Then develop familiarity on the most common principles. Once again, it’s important to understand the basic landscape of the field to establish a strong context for your learning, which makes expertise easier to attain.

Go slower than you think you need to. One of the most frustrating things about learning a musical instrument is when one can’t replicate a piece of music exactly the way they first heard it played, especially when it’s at a quick tempo.

Thus, a particularly effective method to increasing your musical proficiency is rehearsing a given piece slowly. I mean really slowly. I’m talking glacially slow. Anywhere from half the normal speed all the way down to twenty or even ten percent of the pace.
The difference is how you pay attention to mistakes. And this speaks to the idea of being patient, allowing yourself to stay on a certain topic that you haven't quite understood fully.
If you attempt to rush, you’ll inevitably end up with self-created knowledge gaps that could be damaging.
When you reach a part in your study that isn’t quite connecting with you, stay with it and work on it until it does.

One of the best things about being an expert is that it’s so much easier for you to actually resemble an expert. It’s true! In just a few quick lessons, you, too, can appear to be a world-class brainiac and master of intellect! Call now and you’ll receive a turtleneck sweater absolutely free! It sounds like it would fit in right along with late-night infomercials for rotisserie ovens and making passive income by working at home.
But creating the perception among others that you’re an expert has some fringe benefits.

Join two or three related trade organizations. Read the three top-selling books on your topic. Give one free one-to-three-hour seminar at the closest well-known university. Give two free seminars at branches of well-known companies. Offer to write one or two articles for trade magazines. Join ProfNet—a service that journalists use to find experts to quote for articles

Go where you’re needed. Self-promotion is like all other forms of advertising: it’s based on finding the right market and flooding it with your image. Your expertise is now part of your image. So your directive is to find where someone with your expertise would be needed or wanted, and make yourself a universal and popular presence.

Ask yourself: what are the markets for your expertise? What places are receptive to your kind of abilities, talents, and know-how? Where are the people who would appreciate and need you? And how do you make yourself so well-known that you’re practically unavoidable?

title: Manjushri
author: Alicia Jia Dong and Amir Khalilov Abilullin

highlights.text: Some people say practicing Manjushri is about chanting a mantra: “Om Ah Ra Pa Tsa Na Dhi.” “Am I saying it right?” “How many times should I recite it?” Mantras are powerful. But if all you do is recite them mindlessly, without awareness in your daily life, then Manjushri won’t truly appear in your world. I’ve seen people chant thousands of mantras a day, yet not diminish a single delusion—because they treat the mantra as a task, not as a key to awakening.

This book is not here to tell you “how to get smarter.” It’s here to walk with you as you discover: seeing the truth isn’t something to fear. It’s actually a deep form of relaxation. You’re no longer dragged around by emotion, or hijacked by other people’s opinions. You begin to feel that power inside that says, “I see. I know what to do.”

You may wonder: will cultivating wisdom make me cold, overly rational, or emotionally detached? Actually, the opposite is true. A truly wise person is deeply compassionate—not in the superficial sense of just “being nice,” but with a deeper trust: “I believe in your ability to face this. I won’t interfere, but I’ll stand by you.” Manjushri’s wisdom isn’t cold-hearted detachment—it’s a kind of penetrating gentleness.

At the age of 29, the prince made a momentous decision. He renounced his royal title and familial ties, quietly leaving the palace in the dead of night to embark on the path of spiritual practice. In the beginning, he sought out renowned teachers and engaged in deep meditation and ascetic practices.

His first sermon was delivered at the Deer Park in Sarnath to five ascetics, where he expounded on the Four Noble Truths, establishing the foundational structure of Buddhist doctrine. In his later years, he entered parinirvāṇa in Kushinagar, peacefully demonstrating the ultimate state of Nirvana and fulfilling the great vow of his life.

Four Noble Truths: duḥkha (suffering), samudaya (origin), nirodha (cessation), and mārga (path). These truths form the very framework of the Dharma and explain why Buddhism centers on the goal of "liberation from the ocean of suffering."

Life is inherently marked by suffering. This does not mean that life holds no joy or value, but rather that it is inevitably accompanied by forms of pain: birth, aging, illness, death, separation from loved ones, encounters with those we dislike, unfulfilled desires, and the burden of the five aggregates.

The source of suffering lies in the accumulation of afflictions and attachments. Due to avidyā (ignorance of the truth), people cling to the notion of a self and chase external pleasures rooted in the five desires, creating karma that perpetuates the cycle of rebirth.
Since suffering arises from attachment and affliction, the cessation of suffering is possible when these are eliminated.

How can one move toward the cessation of suffering? The Buddha offered the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

In the Saṃyukta Āgama, a monk once asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the foundation of liberation?” The Buddha replied: “To know suffering, to abandon its origin, to realize its cessation, and to cultivate the path.” In just eight concise characters (in Chinese), the sequence of Buddhist practice is laid out.

In the vast system of Buddhist practice, wisdom (Sanskrit: Prajñā, transliterated as "Prajna") is revered as the core force leading to liberation. It is the luminous awareness that transcends birth and death and directly perceives the true nature of reality. The Buddha taught the Threefold Training—morality (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā)—as the path to liberation, with wisdom being the ultimate destination, symbolizing the insight and clarity that free one from the darkness of afflictions.

The Buddha repeatedly emphasized in the scriptures that spiritual cultivation must follow the Threefold Training of morality, concentration, and wisdom. The Saṃyukta Āgama states: “Morality gives rise to concentration, concentration gives rise to wisdom—thus the Threefold Training.”
Śīla (Morality) involves purifying the body, speech, and mind.
Upholding moral precepts restrains desires and calms the mind, enabling it to settle and develop concentration and wisdom.

“Morality is the root, wisdom is the ultimate.” Without purity of conduct, true wisdom cannot be attained. Just as a muddy pond cannot reflect the moon, without moral clarity, the light of wisdom cannot shine. Morality is the clear water; wisdom is the moonlight reflected upon it.
Samādhi (Concentration) refers to focused and tranquil mental states. It is the training to cut off distractions and mental agitation.
Concentration functions like a refining fire, removing impurities of affliction and allowing the mind’s innate brightness to emerge.
Prajñā (Wisdom) is the clear seeing of reality as it is. It breaks through ignorance and penetrates the emptiness of all phenomena.
“A person with wisdom is like someone with eyes—they do not lose their way in darkness”
highlights.note: There is deep clarity there.

highlights.text: If morality is the boat and concentration is the propelling force, wisdom is the guiding light that leads to the other shore. Wisdom does not arise spontaneously—it develops through the continuous cultivation of morality and concentration.

It is not the accumulation of worldly knowledge but the realization that “the five aggregates are empty, thus overcoming all suffering.” Its function is to see through appearances to their essence, to grasp the truths of suffering, its cause, cessation, and the path, and to understand the roots of samsara and liberation.

Prajñā is the central form of wisdom in Buddhism. As one of the Pāramitās ("perfections"), it is the heart of the path to Buddhahood. Prajñā is not knowledge or logical reasoning—it is a non-dual, direct realization beyond words and thought.

Dīrgha Āgama, “Ignorance is the basis; volitional formations arise conditioned by it.” It is the first link in the twelve links of dependent origination, indicating that without breaking ignorance, beings remain adrift in the ocean of suffering.
explains: “Ignorance means not understanding the Four Noble Truths, dependent origination, the Three Jewels, or the law of karma.”
For instance, after the Buddha’s parinirvana, Ānanda, upon reflecting deeply, overcame subtle attachment to self and attained arhatship—an embodiment of wisdom shattering ignorance.
“Not arising, not ceasing; not permanent, not annihilated; not the same, not different; not coming, not going.” These articulate the prajñā perspective on emptiness.

“One should give rise to a mind that does not abide anywhere.” Within emptiness arises boundless compassion, free from attachment to merit. The marvel of prajñā is in breaking clinging without falling into nihilism, in engaging with the world without being stained by it.
Prajñā is not an abstract theory but a practical and experiential path.
Theravāda Buddhism similarly emphasizes vipassanā (insight meditation), observing body and mind to directly perceive impermanence, suffering, and non-self—ultimately realizing non-self directly.

Prajñā is not just for personal liberation—it is the foundation of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva’s altruistic path. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra states: “Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Buddhas.” The Bodhisattva takes prajñā as essence and compassion as function—applying wisdom and compassion together to benefit all beings.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra describes Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva guiding future Buddhas with the light of prajñā, inspiring their aspiration and practice.

Historically, masters like Zhiyi, Xuanzang, and Tsongkhapa are paragons of integrated wisdom. Xuanzang’s translation of the 600-volume Prajñā Sutra revealed the principle of “emptiness as mere designation,” blending logical rigor with profound meditative realization, and spreading prajñā thought widely throughout China.

Many contemporary practice groups have adopted mindfulness meditation as a vehicle for prajñā, such as Pa-Auk Sayadaw and Ajahn Chah in the Theravāda tradition, who integrate the insight of dependent origination and emptiness into breath awareness, helping practitioners directly perceive impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

Within the vast Dharma, wisdom is the core of liberation, the power that transcends all illusions. From morality arises concentration, from concentration arises wisdom—wisdom dispels illusions and reveals truth, leading to the path of emptiness.

liberation. In the Theravada tradition, wisdom primarily focuses on the realization of "no-self," the "Four Noble Truths," and "dependent origination," with the ultimate goal being the attainment of arahantship.

Therefore, wisdom in Mahayana Buddhism not only illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena but also generates boundless compassion for sentient beings. Its development forms a system of liberation that unites philosophy, faith, and practice.

Mahayana Buddhism is guided by the principle that "wisdom is the eye, and great compassion is the heart" in practice. Without wisdom, the compassion of the Bodhisattva would be reduced to mere emotional flow; without compassion, wisdom would lose its motivation and fall into cold indifference.
In the Prajnaparamita Sutras, it is clearly stated: "If a Bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they always accompany it with great compassion, never abandoning sentient beings."

For instance, Avalokiteshvara, in the Guanyin Sutra, manifests thirty-three different forms to respond to the needs of various beings, saving them according to their specific circumstances. This compassionate action is rooted in wisdom, which perceives the suffering of sentient beings, understands the emptiness of all phenomena, and, without attachment to form, continues to liberate beings.

In Mahayana philosophy, "no-self" is not only a cognitive deconstruction but also a transformation of the practitioner's character: shifting from an ego-centered existence to one that is rooted in the existence of all beings. As stated in the Bodhisattvabhumi: "May I become a Buddha for the benefit of all beings." This statement encapsulates the harmony of compassion and wisdom.
"Without the great aspiration for bodhicitta, even if one attains direct realization of emptiness, they will not enter the Mahayana path."
light. A Mahayana practitioner uses wisdom to perceive emptiness and break the attachment to the self, while they use compassion and altruistic vows to benefit others, walking the Bodhisattva path.

The most distinctive practice in Mahayana Buddhism is the "Bodhisattva Path." This path, with the goal of "self-realization and benefiting others," transcends the singular liberation approach of the Theravada tradition and moves towards universal care and collective liberation.

The primary practice in the Bodhisattva path is the "Six Perfections" (ṣaṭpāramitā): generosity, morality, patience, effort, concentration, and wisdom. Among these, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the most important, guiding the other five towards the ultimate goal of Nirvana.

Only wisdom, like a sharp sword, can cut through the attachments to self and phenomena, ensuring that the other perfections are free from defilement. Thus, without wisdom, generosity may lead to pride, morality may become rigid, and meditation may result in a form of detachment. Only wisdom can guide all actions, ensuring that they are not stained by attachment.

action. In the Vimalakīrti Sutra, the lay practitioner Vimalakīrti teaches the great arhats and Bodhisattvas using the non-dual path, explaining that one should not separate worldly reality from ultimate truth, nor should one differentiate between affliction and enlightenment, birth and death, or samsara and Nirvana.
Since the suffering of the world is real, without the foundation of emptiness, a compassionate practitioner could become overwhelmed by the ocean of suffering.
Mahayana practitioners, guided by wisdom, see the world as an illusion, yet still work to alleviate the suffering of others through their compassionate efforts.
highlights.note: Because we are caught in this illusion and think it's real.

highlights.text: says: "One should not dwell anywhere when generating the mind." This implies that a Bodhisattva must act without attachment to their actions. Not clinging to merit, forms, or the consequences of their actions, a Bodhisattva is guided by the wisdom of emptiness in their interactions with the world.
highlights.note: How do you do this?

highlights.text: Its central concept is "the emptiness of all phenomena," advocating that "all phenomena are empty, neither existent nor nonexistent, neither coming nor going." The sutra aims to eradicate attachment to the idea of fixed entities and selfhood.
Emptiness does not negate existence but affirms the interdependent origination of all phenomena, rejecting clinging to the notion of inherent existence.

Nāgārjuna is regarded as the "common ancestor of all eight schools," systematizing the wisdom of emptiness through his Madhyamaka philosophy. He transcended debates between the Mahayana and Theravada schools, elevating the concept of emptiness to a philosophical system that underscores the universal significance of dependent origination.

Manjushri is the Bodhisattva of wisdom, frequently appearing in the Avatamsaka Sutra to assist novice Bodhisattvas in realizing the nature of ultimate reality. In the Manjushri Nirvāna Sutra, Manjushri uses numerous skillful means to help his disciples eliminate ego-attachment, demonstrating the boundless application of wisdom.

In his work The Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment, he outlines how to cultivate wisdom through study and practice, ultimately leading to the realization of non-attachment and the full achievement of Buddhahood.

In Mahayana Buddhism, wisdom is not merely intellectual or abstract speculation but involves a deep transformation of life and behavior. From the empty view of understanding to the compassionate action in practice, wisdom on the Mahayana path unfolds in a comprehensive and integrated manner.
Within the Buddhist framework, all afflictions are ultimately rooted in "ignorance."

Therefore, the “wisdom” spoken of in Buddhism aims to correct this existential delusion and to dissolve our misapprehension of reality. From this we understand that cultivating wisdom is not about gaining more intellectual resources or analytical power, but about dispelling illusion and revealing truth, aligning our inner perception with the Dharma-nature of the universe.

The modern person faces various afflictions—anxiety, anger, desire, frustration, jealousy, loneliness… These are not abstract philosophical puzzles but real, recurring experiences in our everyday lives. However, from the perspective of Buddhist wisdom, none of these afflictions originate from “others” or from “external circumstances,” but from our own inner attachments and fixed views.

For example, when one suffers deeply after losing a loved one, the pain does not arise from the loss itself, but from our attachment to permanence and possession. When someone insults us and we become angry, that emotion is not caused by the words themselves but by our excessive identification with the “self” and our instinct to defend it.
The Buddha did not teach us to repress these emotions, but to observe them with wisdom and understand their causes.

view.” This kind of “contemplation” is not a theoretical understanding but a vivid observation of how our emotions, thoughts, and actions arise from causes and conditions—and how they expand into suffering due to clinging.

Wisdom is this power of inward observation. It is not a cold and distant detachment, nor a purely logical analysis, but a gentle yet steadfast gaze that allows us to generate insight into the true nature of life’s phenomena.
highlights.note: Hence admiring your 3 pure centers. Not forcing energy into them.

highlights.text: The Buddha’s teachings ultimately point toward liberation—a state of freedom that transcends the cycle of birth and death and is no longer bound by afflictions. This state is not a mystical realm but a natural clarity reached through wisdom. The Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra states: “All Buddhas are rooted in wisdom; without wisdom, no wholesome qualities can be accomplished.”

If a practitioner only develops moral discipline and meditative concentration, they may attain mental peace, but it is difficult to uproot fundamental ignorance. Only Prajñā-wisdom, like a sharp sword, can cut through attachment to self and to phenomena. Only then can afflictions be eradicated at the root, rather than temporarily suppressed.
wisdom: all things arise through conditions, and none have intrinsic nature—this “emptiness of self-nature” is the key to liberation.

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood issues among practitioners. Modern society encourages the pursuit of knowledge—we are trained from a young age to “know more” and to equate understanding with wisdom. Even in some Buddhist circles, there is an overemphasis on doctrinal interpretation and a neglect of actual practice, with the mistaken belief that reciting sutras, memorizing doctrines, or mastering debate qualifies one as “wise.” But the wisdom taught by the Buddha is categorically different from knowledge (Vidya) or logic (Tarka).
Knowledge involves gathering information and using language, text, and concepts to describe and categorize the world.

In the Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra, Mañjuśrī asks the layman Vimalakīrti: “What is the path of the Buddha?” Vimalakīrti replies: “The path of the Buddha is inexpressible.” The point here is that the Buddha’s path is not a logical system nor a conceptual framework, but a state of awareness beyond language.

This wisdom does not deny logic—it transcends its limitations. For example, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings suffering, they do not use logic to determine whether the suffering is “beneficial” or “deserved” before deciding whether to help. Instead, they act from great compassion born of emptiness, and from the non-dual realization, they enter the world to serve.

This holistic intuition of wisdom does not arise from thinking, but matures naturally through meditative calm, insight, mindfulness, and the cultivation of Prajñā. Like a clear reflection of the moon in still water, wisdom is the natural radiance of a purified mind.

a) Wisdom Born of Listening: Gained by hearing, reading, and discussing sutras and commentaries to establish right view This is the preliminary stage, preventing one from falling into wrong views such as eternalism or nihilism. While not ultimate wisdom, it prepares the soil for its emergence—like turning the earth before planting seeds.

Using rational thought to clarify concepts and establish an understanding of causality and emptiness Like fertilizing and watering crops, this involves deepening one's understanding of the Dharma through reasoning.

This is the genuine realization of wisdom. Through meditation, one directly contemplates the impermanence of the five aggregates, the non-self of conditioned existence, and the emptiness of all phenomena. In inner observation and mindfulness, false attachments are peeled away, revealing innate clarity. At this point, wisdom arises not from thought but from the mind’s own luminous nature.

Transforming Consciousness into Wisdom: From discriminative thinking to Prajñā-intuition Buddhism speaks of “transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms.” The sixth consciousness is the center of discriminative thought, which delights in analyzing and judging. Prajñā, however, is the direct intuition of “nothing to gain.” Through practice, the originally afflicted and clinging mind is gradually transformed into pure, unobstructed wisdom.

“All sentient beings possess the wisdom and virtues of the Tathāgata, but cannot realize them due to false thoughts and attachments.” This shows that wisdom is not externally acquired but innately present. Afflictions themselves are simply wisdom in deluded form. If one transforms consciousness into wisdom, then affliction itself becomes bodhi (awakening).
“Wisdom” is not cold rationality, nor is it a transcendent intellectual system. It is the living flame of awakened life.

Buddhas.” Mañjuśrī appears frequently in the Buddhist scriptures as an assistant to the Buddha’s wisdom and, within practice traditions, becomes a crucial focus for practitioners in contemplating reality and awakening prajñā.
Riding a lion: The lion, king of beasts, symbolizes fearless wisdom and spiritual majesty. Riding it signifies that Mañjuśrī subdues all afflictions and conquers demons through the power of wisdom.

Sword of wisdom: This is not a weapon of violence, but the sharp blade of prajñā, cutting through delusion and attachment. It represents the “cutting” power of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom: destroying ego-clinging, attachment to phenomena, and dualistic extremes.
Prajñā scripture: Symbolizes the fundamental wisdom he teaches. The Prajñāpāramitā texts and Madhyamaka treatises are regarded as teachings infused with Mañjuśrī’s wisdom.

Crown of five Buddhas: Symbolizes the integration of the Five Wisdoms: the Wisdom of the Dharmadhātu, the Great Mirror Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, the Discerning Wisdom, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Activities.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra is a key Mahāyāna text exploring the emptiness of prajñā and nondual wisdom. Vimalakīrti, a layman, displays great spiritual powers and expounds profound prajñā. None of the great disciples dares to debate him—only Mañjuśrī steps forward, revealing his unobstructed wisdom.

In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Mañjuśrī serves as a mentor for novice bodhisattvas, especially in the chapter “Entering the Dharma Realm,” where he guides the youth Sudhana on a pilgrimage of fifty-three encounters. Each visit represents the unfolding of a particular Dharma teaching, with Mañjuśrī serving as both the point of origin and destination—symbolizing the awakening and ultimate refuge in wisdom.

says: “If one wishes to practice prajñā, one must abandon all appearances, and even the idea of abandonment must not be grasped.” This deepens the Diamond Sūtra’s line “Let the mind arise without dwelling on anything,” pointing to the need to transcend even the notion of detachment to truly enter the state of non-attainment and pure contemplation.

education: In modern education, knowledge transmission dominates. Mañjuśrī’s wisdom reminds us that true education lies in awakening the ability to see, not in indoctrination. A wise person is not one who knows a lot, but one who sees clearly.
Mañjuśrī’s wisdom is not the sum of information, nor mere reasoning ability—it is a quality of mind, a fundamental transformation in the way we exist.
Through Mañjuśrī, we learn how to “attain by non-attaining,” how to “practice all virtue without clinging to dharmas,” and how to “dwell in light amid ignorance.”

In Sanskrit, “Mañju” means “gentle,” “pure,” or “beautiful,” while “śrī” denotes “radiance,” “auspiciousness,” or “merit.” Therefore, “Mañjuśrī” is often interpreted as “Wonderful Auspiciousness” or “Sublime Virtue.”

1. Sublime Virtue: The Seamless Integration of Morality and Wisdom “Sublime Virtue” does not merely indicate noble character but refers to the full embodiment of perfected qualities in Buddhist terms.

In the Mañjuśrī’s Nirvana Sutra, the Buddha says: “Mañjuśrī is the exemplar of all virtues, the foremost in wisdom.” This statement highlights that Mañjuśrī is not only the pinnacle of wisdom but also guides beings with skillful virtue, fully embodying both wisdom and merit.
“Wonderful Auspiciousness” is a symbol of blessing, not merely indicating luck or good fortune but expressing the religious aspiration for transcendental wisdom.

As the deity of “Wonderful Auspiciousness,” Mañjuśrī signifies that the wisdom he manifests brings ultimate happiness to beings. Wisdom is not just sharp discernment of truth, but also a compassionate and skillful means that inspires faith and leads deluded beings toward liberation.

Through the image of Mañjuśrī, we catch a glimpse of the Buddhist understanding of “wisdom” — not as abstract speculation removed from life, nor as mere intellectual accumulation, but as a luminous, compassionate, non-attached way of being.

“Wonderful Auspiciousness” is not just a name, but a state of wisdom: unattached to form, unbound by doctrine, deeply aware of dependent origination, compassionate toward all beings, and practicing prajñā free from grasping. To understand Mañjuśrī is to understand the Buddhist ideal of wisdom. To venerate Mañjuśrī is to venerate our own innate potential for awakening. To cultivate the path of Mañjuśrī is to realize, in our lives, the possibility of truth and direct insight into our true nature.

The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom states: “Wisdom is like a sharp sword that can cut through ignorance.” Mañjuśrī’s sword represents the bodhisattva’s ability to sever the root causes of suffering — greed, anger, ignorance, and deluded thoughts. It is not a tool for harming life, but a metaphor for “slaying the demon of ignorance” and overcoming attachments to views and dharmas.

Flaming blade: symbol of destroying dualistic clinging The sword is often depicted surrounded by flames, symbolizing the intense and brilliant power of wisdom that burns away self-attachment and dharma-attachment — the two root delusions. Artistically, it expresses the Madhyamaka philosophy: “To refute existence and non-existence without asserting anything — that is the Middle Way.” The sword of Mañjuśrī is the artistic embodiment of this middle path wisdom.

Buddhism often refers to the bodhisattva as the “Lion King,” meaning wisdom leads all virtues. Among the six perfections (pāramitās), prajñā is supreme and guides generosity, ethics, and other practices toward liberation. Mañjuśrī’s lion mount shows how wisdom governs and harmonizes all Dharma practices.

Only then did he understand: the beggar who had twice saved his life on the journey was not an ordinary man, but Manjushri himself, unwilling to let Xuyun die before fulfilling his vow. In hindsight, the first rescue in the snow was a test of his initial resolve; the second, during a severe illness, tested the depth of his filial heart. Having passed both trials, Xuyun finally reached the sacred site, completing his mission.
"Bodhi originally has no tree, the mirror has no stand; originally there is not a single thing — where can dust alight?"

Each time a powerful emotion arises is an excellent opportunity to initiate observation—just as the saying goes: “When demons arise, be aware of them; when they leave, realize their emptiness.” As soon as emotional demons arise, be mindful; as they fade, understand their lack of inherent self-nature.

If we are caught in anger, desire, or grief and cannot pull ourselves out, we are in the grip of affliction. But if in the next moment we suddenly awaken and recognize these emotions as fleeting illusions, and release our attachment, then the mind is immediately liberated and wisdom manifests.

A sincere practitioner treats every “minor” event in life as a lesson in self-cultivation. When praised, they practice humility; when criticized, they practice non-anger; in favorable conditions, they cultivate gratitude; in adversity, they learn wisdom and endurance.
This confirms that “affliction is bodhi” is not mere rhetoric—when approached with the right attitude, our painful emotions become our greatest teachers.

Every emotional storm is an invitation to practice the Dharma Gate of Nonduality. Every trial or hardship is a direct test pointing us inward. If we can face both pleasure and pain, craving and aversion with equanimity, and remain centered amid emotional turbulence—observing the mind without being swept away—then afflictions will lose their grip over us and return to their original empty, peaceful nature.
This is the essence of Satipaṭṭhāna: to observe the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects not with judgment, but with clear awareness.

Regardless of which method you choose, the attitude must be both gentle and resolute. “Gentle” means not fighting with thoughts, not berating yourself for having too many. “Resolute” means not giving up or drifting along with distractions, but continuing to train mindfulness and clarity.

Many Chan masters liken mind training to taming an ox: one hand holds the whip (reminding yourself to be mindful), the other holds grass (treating the mind with care). Or like tuning a string—too tight and it breaks, too loose and it makes no sound. If we are too harsh, forcing the mind into silence, we may develop tension or even psychological resistance. If we are too lax, the mind remains wild and unfocused.

First, we must accept that the path of cultivation is not a straight, ever-ascending line. More often, it's two steps forward and one step back—winding and nonlinear. Today's sense of stagnation doesn't mean you haven't progressed, nor does it mean future advancement is impossible. In fact, the plateau offers a valuable chance to pause and reevaluate the direction and methods of your practice.

Whatever your motivation was, now is the time to reaffirm and deepen it. Mahāyāna teachings stress the centrality of bodhicitta—the mind of awakening—as the root of all virtuous practice. As The Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras explains, when bodhicitta declines, all other qualities wither.

So, sit quietly and renew your vow: “May I practice the Dharma diligently in this life to transcend birth and death, and bring benefit to all beings. Temporary boredom or hardship cannot stop me from moving toward awakening.”
Aspiration is like a lamp—it can illuminate even the darkest moments of your inner world. When the lamp of motivation is relit, your practice regains its meaning, and renewed energy arises.

Another cause of stagnation is repetitive monotony—a kind of spiritual fatigue from overly rigid or one-dimensional routines. In such cases, consider varying your schedule or introducing different forms of practice.
Reflect: Have I only been practicing but not studying, leaving me without fresh insight? Or am I studying excessively and not embodying what I read?

Also consider whether a lack of merit is at play. The path relies not only on wisdom and method but also on puṇya (merit). If you've been practicing alone for a long time without engaging in acts of generosity or service, inner dryness can arise. Step outside your bubble: serve others, volunteer, help your family, donate, release animals.

Many practitioners report that serving at a Dharma center during a plateau re-energized them. Once they returned to the cushion, obstacles had mysteriously vanished. Balance ethics, concentration, wisdom, and merit. This well-rounded approach helps us break through plateaus with grace.

Sometimes, plateaus arise because we’ve grown too comfortable—practice becomes routine, no longer demanding growth. Life may “cooperate” by introducing challenges: illness, setbacks, or disappointment. Don’t resist them—use adversity to deepen your practice.

This is real-life training. As the Platform Sūtra says, “True awakening is not apart from the world.” It’s not found only in remote caves, but in responding to everyday joys and sufferings with a transformed heart.

If adversity doesn’t naturally appear, create challenges yourself: Go on a short retreat to break habits of laziness. Make a pilgrimage, or undertake an intensive repentance or devotional practice. Consciously face a fear or aversion (within reason and safety).

The scriptures warn: “He who travels a hundred miles sees ninety as only halfway.” The closer we are to real transformation, the stronger the resistance may feel. We must press on. Remember the examples of great masters: The Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree undisturbed by Mara’s illusions, attaining enlightenment through unwavering resolve. Bodhidharma meditated facing a wall for nine years before transmitting the Dharma to China. Milarepa practiced in solitude for years, tempted to quit—but he endured, and attained liberation.

Often, breakthroughs happen at the moment when we’re about to give up. A new clarity, a subtle joy, a quiet insight may suddenly arise—and the long darkness vanishes. That single moment will re-ignite your heart.
Even if no dramatic state arises, if you maintain precepts and avoid major errors, you are still accumulating the causes for awakening.

And in all this—be kind to yourself. Plateaus may bring frustration or self-blame. But compassion begins with you. Say to yourself: “I’ve come this far—that alone is incredible. Now I’m simply pausing, catching my breath, before I continue.” Allow yourself rest. Go for a walk in nature. Let your nervous system soften. Recall the story of Sona, a monk who meditated so hard he injured his feet, then wanted to quit. The Buddha taught him the lute-string simile: if the string is too tight, it breaks; too loose, and it won’t play. Sona adjusted his effort and attained Arhatship.

Plateaus are not obstacles to be feared, but essential lessons on the path. What matters is your attitude and response. Examine the causes with wisdom. Adjust skillfully. Seek guidance. Rekindle aspiration. Stay steady and flexible. The two keys to crossing a plateau are persistence and adaptability: keep going without giving up, but be willing to change your approach. Each time you pass through one of these phases, your mind becomes stronger, more mature, more resilient.

harbors no obsession with people, no bias toward events—his heart is like an orchid blooming quietly in a secluded valley, fragrant yet unbound. This freedom from attachment brings lightness of heart and allows him to face the ever-changing world with grace.

Knowing that everyone has tender and vulnerable parts within, the wise practitioner approaches others with kindness and patience. His speech is gentle but powerful; in conflict, he favors understanding and tolerance over argument.
The gentleness of the wise is the outward expression of this humility. His presence is like spring rain, quietly nurturing, bringing comfort and ease to those around him.

Taken together, these four qualities shape the inner landscape of the wise practitioner: non-attachment brings freedom, gentleness fosters warmth, steadfastness ensures powerful practice, and compassion opens the heart to others. His mind is like the vast sky—open and unobscured by clouds of clinging; his heart, like fertile earth—nurturing the flowers of kindness and wisdom.
Wisdom is not merely a lofty idea found in deep meditation or scripture—it is intimately connected to everyday life and can serve as a guiding light in every moment.
First, in relationships, wisdom allows one to “see deeply without judging.” To see deeply means perceiving the true needs and hidden pain behind others’ behaviors.

Next, in career and life choices, wisdom enables one to “see the essence and release attachment.” In our competitive world, many are driven by ambition for wealth or status. But a wise person regularly pauses to ask: What do I truly seek? Is my life path aligned with my deepest values and long-term well-being? To “see the essence” means looking past appearances to the deeper significance of things.
In emotional matters, wisdom helps us grasp the nature of arising and passing—knowing that even deep feelings require thoughtful care, and that clinging leads to suffering.

In times of adversity, wisdom provides a unique strength and openness. When plans unravel or misfortune strikes, we often fall into despair. But the wise remember: “Misfortune may be a hidden blessing.”

At the beginning of their journey, many practitioners may turn to the Dharma out of a desire for personal peace and freedom. Through meditation, study, and contemplation, they gradually dispel ignorance and begin to taste the serene joy that wisdom brings. However, as wisdom matures, a profound realization arises: all sentient beings and the self are fundamentally inseparable.

The compassionate aspiration of the wise practitioner manifests as a powerful arising of bodhicitta—the aspiration to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. Bodhicitta can be simply described as the resolve to seek enlightenment above and to liberate sentient beings below.

They had forgotten that within their flesh grew the seeds of those same powers that made the deer jump in the mountains, the same powers used by tigers on the hunt and by birds in flight. They were so busy studying the sutras that they had forgotten about the sutra written in the body

Even the world would have never been the same had any of the Western prophets been struck by the same intuition that the myth attributes to Bodhidharma. Imagine Jesus Christ preaching after a session of Tai Chi Chuan
I agree completely with Tai Chi master Yang Jwing-Ming when he writes that the world needs Chi Kung as much as it needs a perfect plan for the restoration of global economy.

The moment they ask us to choose between two different paths, the implicit message is that we can only follow one. Either scholars or athletes. Either creative or pragmatic. But the idea that if we want one thing we must renounce something else is one of the worse aberrations ever invented.

I know people who are naturally strong, healthy, and agile, but they are not aware of it. Their bodies possess a wisdom that they can’t access. They are like little gnomes who direct the body from the control room, prisoners within their heads.
As soon as you enter a room, right away you perceive who is an individual from head to toe and who has never listened to the voice of the body.
Reading body language is not the result of practice, nor is it a technique that can be taught. It is something that happens naturally when mind and body don’t fight each other.
We are reminded of the body only when it hurts. It is portrayed as a source of suffering, as a negative entity giving people pain and trouble.
Our equipment is simply much too sophisticated for us to know what to do with it. Our bodies are the kingdoms of lost continents and unknown lands.
The fascination many people have for “supernatural” phenomena is the result of their lack of deep knowledge of what Nature is about.
Few things are as psychedelic as the concept of Chi. All internal arts are based on the development of an energy that cannot be seen, touched, or perceived by any of the senses.

I have to admit that seeing great psychedelic potentials at a time when your legs are ready to apply for an early retirement and your mind is wandering trying to find something to distract it from pain may not be easy.

Musashi and Sun Tzu couldn’t be any more different from each other, but both The Book of Five Rings by Musashi and The Art of War by Sun Tzu are authentic masterpieces teaching how to face conflict in order to live beyond conflict: not simply martial arts strategy, but strategy of life.
For this reason, truly understanding the strategy of combat means understanding how to face reality rather than endure it.
Reality has no secrets for those who can penetrate it with their sight.

The strategy of martial arts begins by looking around and reading the state of things. If more people trusted their own perceptions, priests and new age gurus would be unemployed. The ability to observe is as simple as it is rare because most people prefer believing in just about anyone else rather than in themselves

They are unconscious prisoners of a very vicious karmic cycle. In this context, emotions are not the result of a choice, but of automatic responses. With the hammer, the doctor softly hits a nerve under the knee, and the leg reacts with a kick. Many people face life without any more awareness than Pavlov’s dogs. Constantly manipulated by external stimuli, they end up as hostages in the hands of events beyond their control.
The one winning the conflict is not the one who is strongest, but the one who knows how to control the opponent emotionally.
They stop being chess pieces that can be moved by other people’s actions. Free from automatic responses, they don’t jump as soon as someone waves a red flag under their nose. They are in control.

Rather than being pushed left and right by other people’s words and actions, we get to choose which path to follow. To quit being defenseless doesn’t mean becoming insensitive. We simply stop being the bull whose destiny is to lose. Rather than charging blindly, we can choose how to respond.

Once we find out that we are free to choose, we can become designers of our own lives. We become at the same time the artist and the masterpiece. The game begins by observing one’s natural reactions to the events taking place in daily life. It is not a bad psychoanalytic trip.
Taoism, the philosophical soul at the roots of many styles of martial arts, views open conflict as the last choice after all others have failed.
If accepting a challenge is not worth it, diverting others’ aggressiveness is a good way to avoid wasting energy in useless conflicts.
If you don’t give up your power and your dignity, no one can take it from you.
Michael Jordan, the Buddha, and the best warriors all possess the same frightening self-confidence: the ability to come out as winners before a single word is pronounced or an action is taken.
The power of a warrior to dominate conflict is the best guarantee of avoiding conflict. In order to live in peace, one needs the strength to win a war.
If a myth spreads through time and space, it is because it possesses something that touches the heart of human beings
The Dragon comes to us in the shape of all the problems we stumble upon in daily life. It is the force that constantly stands between us and the fulfillment of our desires.

The hero must be an expert in the art of war in order to win in this conflict. The hero is pure yang energy. Assertiveness, strength, bravery, an indomitable will, and the skill of a god in the midst of battle are the Warrior’s tools.
One of humanity’s tragedies is that most people have lost (or just never had) the capacity to be warriors and princesses, and settled for being the shadows of what they could be.
Thanks to martial arts, women have the occasion to come in contact with their long-repressed yang energy and physical power without having to turn into androgynous-looking, steroid-fed machines.
If you know how to fight, peace is a choice. In this way, a woman can stop seeing herself as weak and defenseless in both body and character.

The essential attribute of the Warrior is the refusal to give away one’s power. Family, friends, schoolteachers, political parties, churches, gangs … the catalogue of volunteers willing to influence our decisions is longer than I can list.

The Warrior eats up an army for breakfast because the Warrior is an individual, whereas the army is made up of numbers and “yes sirs” whose character and individuality are repressed by the necessity to subordinate to the military machine

Being responsible doesn’t mean sacrificing our freedom on the altar of Duty. It means doing anything to make our lives worthy of our dreams. The quintessence of the Warrior is in swearing loyalty to one’s own visions.

Everything that we can see and touch is there because we accept it to be so. Our houses, the state of our physical bodies, our friends, our jobs are all the results of our choices. Once we remember this, it becomes possible to turn into artists of living.

Everyone experiences the conflict between reality and their desires. Those who lack a Warrior’s attitude are left powerless after the first few defeats. Without the Warrior, we are in the hands of fate. Our choices have no power.
Jordan, Kobe, or D’Antoni can make mistakes like any other human being, but the difference is that they don’t ever stop irradiating a feeling of complete confidence.

If the Warrior’s strength doesn’t go hand in hand with the Princess’ grace and sweetness, the Warrior is not much more than an efficient killer (if the Warrior metaphor is taken literally) or a simple problem-solver (if the Warrior image is taken in its widest sense.)

Some of the most mythical warriors populating the Olympus of martial arts have become famous not simply for their legendary feats as fighters, but also for the serenity of their spirits. The descriptions we have of them often coincide: calm, relaxed, peaceful men with a genuine love for life. They walked along the Warrior’s path because it takes an indomitable spirit to be able to live beyond conflict, but once they reached their goals, the fighter’s intensity was put to rest in order to make room for gentleness.
“The way of the warrior is the creation of harmony.”

The practice of martial arts is a ritual that helps me to remember who I am. Remembering who I am is the only thing I really need, but it is a never-ending task, because forgetting is very easy and equally easy is not realizing I have forgotten.
And Deng Ming Dao adds: “Discipline is freedom, and the companion to imagination. Discipline makes it possible for you to become whatever you want to be.”
What inspired the deepest respect was the man, his personality, his example.
No teacher can compare to an idealized all-wise, all-powerful, compassionate yet demanding archetype.

And the reality of martial arts in the daily lives of thousands of practitioners doesn’t seem very spectacular either. They may be deep, powerful, and beautiful beyond words, but they don’t translate well onto a screen.

But at the core of a martial arts movie—no matter how poorly done it may be—is the quest for power, the hero’s journey to develop the qualities that can remove all the obstacles on the way to happiness.
Movies, like martial arts practice itself, could be approached as rituals to get in touch with the heroic qualities we cherish, and help us remember the sacred fire laying dormant within.
Like any other human being, the samurai loves life, but the difference is that to him a life without honor is not worth living.
Demanding from himself a perfection that goes beyond human limits and putting all of his energies into every action are his way of living.
highlights.note: Put your all into everything you do.

highlights.text: Even the power of laws and written contracts fade in comparison with his word, because laws can be bent with shrewdness and contracts can be broken, but his word is more sacred than life itself. The samurai is much more than a formidable warrior.
When a samurai loses balance, strength turns into stiffness and the Bushido turns into a prison.
These things are hard to understand for people who dedicate more time to earning money than to cultivating friendships; people who are part of a society that has forgotten that human nature is tribal
The loneliness, the alienation, the desire for a community plaguing millions of people today are the direct result of having lost the key to tribal living.
Molding our characters in order to become more gracious people in everyday life is already more than most people dream of doing.
But my vision tells me that if the way of the warrior doesn’t give birth to a spiritual revolution shaking the very roots of our way of facing life, we might as well flush it.

The courage of the warrior has nothing to do with displays of machismo or with the rhetoric of football coaches. It is the courage to take destiny in the palm of our hands and become the leader of our own lives, and this is what I love most of all.
Cultivating warrior virtues is not a part-time job: heroes for two hours within a dojo, before going back to a life without magic. Everyday life is the real battlefield.
Although maybe pleasant, ultimately wealth, fame, and power don’t matter much. If our daily experience is not a source of happiness, we are still prisoners of our own existence.
But if we don’t want to join the ranks of the living dead who simply endure life, it is better to stop complaining and expecting somebody else to find the solutions.

Only warriors with sacred fire in their eyes possess the will to get back on their feet after being knocked down time and time again. It is at this point that martial arts come into play. Hidden between the fighting techniques are the tools to forge our character.
In its highest form, the way of the warrior is that of the bodhisattva: putting one’s talent at the service of a superior destiny.

If you don’t change the world, certainly nobody else will. Changing the world has nothing to do with altruism or with trying to be a good Samaritan. Ultimately, since everything is connected, helping others inevitably means helping ourselves. At the highest level, there is no difference between egoism and altruism. It is a karmic ping-pong game. All our actions come back to us.

Why belong to any school of thought—Lee asked—if all that it does is divide us into opposing factions and prevent us from seeing the truth of different points of view? Our reassuring sense of identity—Lee seemed to suggest—is nothing but a comfortable prison shielding us from the intensity of unfiltered experience.
Following this line of thought, Lee argued that no fixed formula could capture the flow of existence. What worked yesterday may not work today.

Epistemological anarchism, in fact, does not attempt to substitute one method with another. Rather, it frees individuals to find their own methods, and invites them to change them at will if, after some time, their discovery stops producing the desired results.

True knowledge, on the other hand, can only be found beyond all opposites. It thrives where yin and yang dance together. It is physical and intellectual at the same time. It is both very funny and deadly serious.

highlights.text: A ryū is a style of fighting, which, by definition, has been passed down for several generations. To the expert eye, members of a particular ryū are instantly recognizable by minor variations in their posture or technique. However, a ryū is much more than just a style. It is a complete methodology for the transmission and preservation of a system. Its durability has proven its viability. A new system, technically, does not become a ryū until the second generation of disciples.
The ryū is an attempt to pass the method of the founder along to his descendants. Its goal is not to teach, but actually to change the individual.

It is for this reason that the entire concept of the ryū is so unpalatable for many modern people. Raised on a philosophy stressing individual worth, they are unable to surrender to something greater.

As was previously mentioned, the proper attitude for a beginner is called nyūnanshin, the pliability of the spirit that allows him to be easily molded. A disciple with nyūnanshin enters a dōjō fully prepared to surrender his ego to the ryū. He leaves, not as a man with new knowledge, but as a completely new person.

A disciple can spend years or even decades mastering these techniques. During this time he is carefully observed by the sensei. Then if, and only if, the master thinks him worthy, will the disciple be introduced to the hiden, the “secret teachings.” This initiation into the inner mysteries of a system has always been reserved for the very few, for it is these techniques that give mastery over other men. No sensei would consider imparting such information to a man he does not trust with his life. (Many old ryū have been lost because the headmaster died prior to transmitting the hiden to a successor.)

At the other extreme, a hiden can be a mental principle so esoteric as to be incomprehensible to the layman, even when explained in clear language. That is all right, for the ryū specializes in teaching things which the average man can neither see nor understand.
The omote is the front, the things which can be seen, and the oku is the hiden, things which are not readily apparent.

Ki no nagashi is a state of exaltation. It feels as if every cell in your body is intensely alive. (You will never see a senior student of any bujutsu using stimulants. They do not need them.) An analogy that perhaps comes close to giving an impression of this feeling is that of an automobile engine that has been blueprinted—it has been disassembled and all of its parts are polished to exact blueprint specifications. When there is a state of ki no nagashi your body feels like such an engine. It is purring along and operating exactly the way it is supposed to. There is no deep and mysterious force involved, unless you call life itself mysterious. Because you are operating very efficiently, there is no wasted motion or thought. Your body moves gracefully and smoothly. So does your mind. This is why this state is called a “flow of ki”—you feel as if you are flowing through life instead of being bounced from one situation to the next.
It is only when your life force becomes deep, quiet, and powerful, like a great river, that it is referred to as ki no nagashi.

When you have developed ki no nagashi, you can flow from target to target during a battle. As you apply your technique to each of these targets, you focus your entire effort on one small point to ensure maximum destruction. This momentary concentration is called kime, “spiritual focus.” The purpose of kime is pure and simple: power. By focusing your strength on one point, you greatly increase effective power. One pound of pressure spread out over a wide area is of little importance, but a needle driven by one pound of force will penetrate deeply.
When you focus your entire being on a task, there must be no conflict.

The result of basic training in any art is a strong, flexible, and relaxed mind and body. If the training has been vigorous, mind and body will be very healthy. The life force will be very high and synchronized. Where the energy of an untrained person will have a sporadic and fragmented quality, the energy of a properly trained man will have cohesiveness and depth.

You start by selecting a single technique and practicing it over and over, not just for days but for years, until you can execute it perfectly. A very rough rule-of-thumb would be ten thousand repetitions for a simple technique. As you engage in this repetition practice, which is known as renshū, you must drive yourself past the point of exhaustion.

Also, the quality of the technique is of great importance. To win only by accident brings relief, not kiai. It is only through winning with a technique of such perfection and beauty that your opponent is powerless to avoid it that you will feel exaltation. The fascinating thing about kiai is that its limits are far beyond what most people consider to be normal. When you achieve kiai, you feel, in addition to exaltation, a sense of great power. This starts a chain reaction. Because of your feeling of power, you relax a little—you are now so good that you do not have to try so hard anymore. This relaxation results in even greater efficiency. The result is a closed loop with positive feedback.

Zanshin, and the ability to achieve it, has a dual value for the warrior. First, because awareness is so heightened, a person in a state of zanshin becomes a very dangerous man. He is capable of reacting with explosive force to even the slightest provocation. Secondly, zanshin offers a measuring stick for progress because it only happens after a perfect technique. Without this, you would never know for sure if you had reached the ultimate level of physical training.

Kiai is something that happens within you—you can create a state of kiai even when alone. Aiki, however, is bringing your kiai to bear upon your opponent. When you have extremely strong ki, so strong that it is classed as kiai, it affects your enemy. Because he senses your tremendous spiritual strength, his own will to attack is weakened. Perhaps the best definition of aiki was given by Takeda Sogaku,22 who said, “Aiki is the art of defeating your opponent with a single glance.”

The first stage in developing aiki consists of learning a new technique and then practicing it with a partner until you can do it correctly. Then you select different partners and continue practicing until you are sure you can execute the technique against anyone. The third stage takes you back to your original partner. Now as you practice he will gradually increase his resistance. He does this slowly, never allowing you to fail. After you can do the technique against his maximum resistance, you repeat the process with other partners. Finally, there will come a time when you know, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that you can use this technique successfully against anyone, no matter how hard they resist it. When you have reached this level, you will naturally start to reduce the amount of effort you put into the technique. You do this because you know you are going to succeed and no longer feel compelled to try so hard.

Aiki is the ultimate state of any martial art. It is not an external show—you do not frighten your enemy by either action or appearance. Rather it is a lack of external show. You do nothing because your opponent is not important enough for you to have to do anything. Your very existence is enough to defeat him.

Over two thousand years ago in the writings of Sun Tzu (see note five in the introduction), Wu Ch’i said, “A battlefield is a land of standing corpses. Those who wish to live will die.” He meant that if you think about self-defense, you are sure to lose because every thought of defense is one less thought of attack. This is why you must drop all thoughts of personal safety and concentrate on destroying your enemy.
