highlights.text: In the Bhakti tradition, the ultimate goal is to cultivate a loving relationship with Bhagavan. This relationship is based on devotion and surrender, and it requires a deep understanding of spiritual principles and practices. As one develops this relationship, they acquire certain spiritual qualities, such as faith, humility, compassion, and detachment.
When we attain the state of Siddha Bhakti, we experience ultimate bliss that is beyond the scope of the senses. This state is called Samadhi.
Shri Krishna has explained in the Bhagavad Gita how thoughts, speech, actions, austerities, knowledge etc., are all sattvic only when performed with a devotional mindset with humility and purity.
The message is not that we should do bhakti and not do anything else. The message is that we should do everything that we do with a bhava of bhakti.
Elevate yourself through your own self. Do not degrade yourself. The mind is your best friend as well as the worst enemy.

But how can we give away our vikaras when they are so deeply ingrained in us? The key is to be consistent in our practice. As long as we are making even small progress, if bhakti is practiced regularly, then it will help us get free from our vikaras. The easiest of all devotional practices is chanting the holy name along with the mindset of surrender.
Bhagavan graces the bhakti yogi with siddha bhakti when the yogi is ready to receive it. We must prepare ourselves and become ready and eligible for it.

up. Just like that, our mind and body have to be ready to receive the divine current of siddha bhakti. And that preparation is what is called Sadhana bhakti. When practiced with sincerity and consistency, it helps us purify ourselves and get rid of all our vikaras like lust, anger, jealousy, hatred, greed, pride, etc. That is the prerequisite for preparing us for Siddha Bhakti.
If we practice sadhana bhakti with sincerity and consistency, Bhagavan will certainly grace us with siddha bhakti.

He is stating that whatever path one chooses to follow to approach Him, He reciprocates with the devotee accordingly. It is not necessary to follow a specific set of rules or rituals to attain His grace. Instead, devotion and surrender to Him is the key.

Narada Muni says that in order to achieve success in bhakti, we should renounce the objects of sensory pleasures. They are the biggest impediments to our progress on this path. In the path of bhakti, sensory pleasures can become a major obstacle to achieving success. They can create attachments and desires that distract us from our spiritual goals and hinder our progress towards Bhagavan.

In order to cultivate love and devotion towards Bhagavan, it is important to renounce the objects of sensory pleasures. This does not mean denying ourselves enjoyment or pleasure, but rather redirecting our energies towards our spiritual practices. This can be done by offering all our activities to Bhagavan.

By renouncing sensory pleasures, we free our minds from distractions and attachments that can impede our spiritual progress. This allows us to focus more fully on our spiritual practices, such as meditation, prayer, and service, which can help us develop a deeper connection with Bhagavan.
The emphasis is on the fact that those who are resolute on the spiritual path have an intellect which has a clear purpose and a singular aim.

As you can see, we again see the importance of ‘consistency’ being reiterated. As long as we are practicing ‘convenient’ devotion, it will only keep us in Sadhana bhakti. Only when we switch to ‘consistent’ bhakti do we have a chance of achieving Siddha bhakti.
Constant chanting of the holy name (Hare Krishna mantra, Om Namo Narayanaya, etc.) is one of the easiest ways of disciplining our mind and getting us towards consistent practice of bhakti.

Most of us think that we need to worship Bhagavan only when we go to a temple or when we stand in front of His image. However, if we realize that Bhagavan is omnipresent, we will understand why we should be worshiping Bhagavan no matter where we are and what we are doing.
The scriptures make it clear that self-effort is necessary to purify the mind, which in turn opens the way for divine grace to flood in and illuminate the seeker's life with joy and light.

Narada Muni is saying that although we will receive divine grace with the help of a guru, it is very difficult to find a true guru. Because such gurus are rare and even if they come in contact with us, many times we will not be able to recognize them as gurus, because of our own impurities and flaws of perception.

As mentioned in the previous shloka, the aspiring student must purify and prepare themselves and have a strong yearning for getting a guru. Then by the grace of Bhagavan, the guru appears. Once that happens, the student needs to have complete faith in the guru and serve the guru and follow the guru’s teachings and that will lead them to the stage where they will receive the divine grace of Bhagavan in the form of Siddha Bhakti.

The story of Kabir and Saint Ramananda teaches us several important morals. First, it highlights the importance of having a guru in one's spiritual journey, even if the student is an elevated soul like Kabir. A guru can provide guidance and support, helping the disciple to make progress on the spiritual path.

He is talking about the close association of a guru who is intimately aware of our nature and our strengths and weaknesses and who we respect and treat with humility and respect. Spiritual evolution happens when we study in such an environment of close association with a guru.

Even Shri Krishna, who was an incarnation of Bhagavan Himself, sought the association of a guru and accepted Sandipani Muni as His guru. Of course, he was the best student ever and learned 64 sciences in 64 days! Sudama was Shri Krishna’s classmate in the gurukul and he asked Shri Krishna why he needed a guru when He himself was the source of all knowledge including the Vedas.

As previously mentioned, a person who desires Bhagavan's love seeks out a guru to guide them on the spiritual path. The key for the seeker is to cultivate a longing for Bhagavan. Shankaracharya emphasizes that even if this longing for liberation is initially weak, it can be intensified by the teacher's grace and by practicing virtues like humility and detachment.

We have to keep in mind that Kusunga doesn’t just mean the company of criminals. It also means the company of people in strong material consciousness or lower levels of consciousness. And it is not just people, but bad books, violent and vulgar movies, vulgar music, nude pictures, anything that aggravates our sensory attachments, are all evil companies.

This story illustrates how even elevated souls, who just have an insignificantly small ripple of desire in their heart, get sucked up in material desires due to Kusanga. In Rishi's case, the Kusunga was just a couple of fish. Just imagine how much we ordinary mortals may get impacted by Kusunga and that too of evil humans?

Know that the deluded man who walks the dreadful path of sense-craving, moves nearer to his ruin with every step. And know this to be true also-that he who walks the path indicated by his teacher, who is his truest well-wisher, and by his own better judgment, reaps the highest fruit of the knowledge of Brahman.

If you really desire liberation, hold the objects of sense-enjoyment at a distance, like poison; and keep drinking in with delight such virtues as contentment, compassion, forgiveness, straightforwardness, tranquility and self-control, as if they were nectar.
One may wonder, who can truly conquer maya? It is the one who relinquishes all attachments, selflessly serves the elevated souls, and frees themselves from the illusion of "I" and "mine."
In order to get into this mindset of surrender to Bhagavan, Narada Muni says that we must first relinquish material attachments and perform selfless service to guru and other elevated souls.

Satsangatve Nissangatvam - By associating with the wise and virtuous, one becomes detached from worldly desires and attachments. Nissangatve Nirmohatvam - Through detachment, one is freed from delusion and confusion caused by the mind and senses. Nirmohatve Nischalatattvam - By being free from delusion, one attains a steady and unwavering mind. Nischalatattve Jivanmuktih - By having a steady mind, one attains liberation while still living, which is known as jivanmukti.

As discussed in earlier Sutras, every time we give in to weakness and sensory attachments, we become weaker. Conversely, when we practice detachment, we become stronger and our energy level increases. Narada explains that this energy should be utilized to serve those who have expanded their consciousness and have become selfless, wise teachers. Not to waste it on those who are selfish and limited.

Those who avoid the world. Earlier Narada Muni had said we can do bhakti even when living in the world. Still, he says, seek out time that we can spend in solitude. That helps us solidify and focus our mind on Bhagavan, which is a fundamental requirement for progress on the spiritual path.
Similarly, the student of yoga should sit in solitude and not be disturbed by worldly-minded people.

When we add water to milk, it gets mixed quickly and easily. That is how our mind is. When we expose it to the world, all sorts of impurities get easily mixed with the mind. However, once we extract butter from that same milk, water can no longer mix in

the West has discovered how to tap so many powerful sources of energy in nature but still remains largely unaware of the tremendous force, even more powerful than nuclear energy, contained within each one of us. As long as this powerful internal energy lies undiscovered, our life is doomed to remain fragmented and purposeless, and we will continue to fall victim to the mental and emotional pressures so characteristic of our age.

Perhaps his most profound teaching was just this: that we each possess within ourselves not only the answer to our own problems but the potential to live our lives on a much higher level than we currently imagine possible

According to the Buddhist teachings, no matter how confused or deluded we may be at the moment, the underlying and essential nature of our being is clear and pure. In the same way that clouds can temporarily obscure but cannot damage the light-giving power of the sun, so too the temporary afflictions of body and mind — our confusion, anxiety, and the suffering they cause — can temporarily obscure but cannot destroy or even touch the fundamentally clear nature of our consciousness
Although tantric practitioners do not neglect creating the same causes as the followers of sutra, they take the future result of full spiritual evolution as the very starting point in their path

Through the proper practice of tantra all of our energies, including the subtle yet very powerful energies we are not ordinarily aware of, are harnessed to accomplish the greatest of all transformations. This is our evolution from an ordinary, limited, and deluded person trapped within the shell of a petty ego into a fully evolved, totally conscious being of unlimited compassion and insight.

The behavior of someone following this path to individual liberation is therefore characterized by extreme self-control. The practitioner posts a strict guard at the door of the senses and is extremely suspicious of whatever wants to enter.
But we rarely deprive ourselves of something for the right reasons. We squeeze ourselves into a state of misery because we think that being miserable is itself somehow worthwhile

On the other hand, if we know how to experience happiness without the polluted attitudes of either grasping attachment or guilt, we can cultivate deeper and deeper levels of this experience and eventually attain the inconceivable happiness of our full human potential.

The fact that he then went on to achieve complete liberation after only one night’s meditation under the Tree of Enlightenment clearly shows that the time was ripe for him to abandon his previous ascetic practices

The only type of person for whom tantra can work is someone who is primarily concerned with benefiting others and sees the tantric path as the quickest and most powerful way of accomplishing this altruistic aim.

To think, as many people do, “Since tantra is the highest path, it is not necessary for me to bother about the preliminary practices” and then jump into the most advanced teachings is both foolish and arrogant; it is also very dangerous
Finally, it is very important to be able to differentiate clearly between the essence of tantra and the cultural forms in which it is currently wrapped

But my point is that we should always bear in mind that tantra is something far deeper than language or custom. What tantra has to teach us is a way of breaking free from all the conditioning that limits our understanding of who we are and what we can become

With the proper understanding of transformation, whatever we do, twenty-four hours a day, can bring us closer to our goal of totality and self-fulfillment. All our actions — walking, eating, and even urinating! — can be brought into our spiritual path

According to Buddhist tantra, we remain trapped within a circle of dissatisfaction because our view of reality is narrow and suffocating. We hold on to a very limited and limiting view of who we are and what we can become, with the result that our self-image remains oppressively low and negative, and we feel quite inadequate and hopeless.

One of the essential practices at all levels of tantra is to dissolve our ordinary conceptions of ourselves and then, from the empty space into which these concepts have disappeared, arise in the glorious light body of a deity: a manifestation of the essential clarity of our deepest being.

Tantric meditational deities should not be confused with what different mythologies and religions might mean when they speak of gods and goddesses. Here, the deity we choose to identify with represents the essential qualities of the fully awakened experience latent within us.
In tantra we focus our attention upon such an archetypal image and identify with it in order to arouse the deepest, most profound aspects of our being and bring them into our present reality

The next thing to realize is that from the time you were born up until now you have manifested in many different ways. None of us is static and unchanging. For example, when you are filled with anger, you look like a demon, while at other times, filled with love, you look like a beautiful angel. None of these manifestations — whether angry, peaceful, jealous, loving, compassionate, stupid, or wise — arises primarily from your body, from your physical form.

Tantric deities symbolize the full development of this blissful wisdom energy and that is why we can say that such a deity — no matter what color it is or how many faces it has — represents the essence of who we are and what we can become

Those people who think badly of themselves, for whatever reasons, become and then remain miserable, while those who can recognize and draw on their inner resources can overcome even the most difficult situations
Deity yoga is one of the most profound ways of lifting our self-image, and that is why tantra is such a quick and powerful method for achieving the fulfillment of our tremendous potential.

We cannot truly see ourselves as possessing a deity’s transparent body of light if we continue to identify so strongly with our gross physical form. And we will never be able to contact the essentially pure nature of our own being if we continue to think that our mind’s fundamental nature is nothing but the delusions and gross conceptions that pass through it.
The more we can identify ourselves as having a body and mind of pure clear light, the more we open ourselves up to the beneficial forces existing inside and outside ourselves

If the mental image we have of ourselves is positive, then our actions are naturally filled with self-confidence, and the impression we make upon others is one of strength and vitality. On the other hand, if we have a low opinion of ourselves, we appear weak and ineffective

Instead of dealing directly with our mind itself and developing an attitude that will transform our experiences for the better, we take a much more superficial approach and try to manipulate our outer circumstances in an attempt to solve our problems

In other words we need to create space, space in which our essentially pure nature can function uninterruptedly. Then, when we employ the tantric techniques of visualizing ourselves as a deity, we will not be pretending. Rather, we will be bringing to the surface the inner, divine qualities that have always existed within the depths of our being.
First comes renunciation: the mind emerging from its ordinary, limiting preoccupations and taking an interest instead in realizing its unlimited, completely liberated potential.

Instead, it is a sign that we are holding on to our religion as we would any ordinary sense object. In other words, by our grasping attitude we have turned a spiritual practice into yet another form of ordinary attachment.

Renunciation is not the same as giving up pleasure or denying ourselves happiness. It means giving up our unreal expectations about ordinary pleasures. These expectations themselves are what turn pleasure into pain. It cannot be said too often that there is nothing wrong with pleasure.

Simply stated, renunciation is the feeling of being so completely fed up with our recurring problems that we are finally ready to turn away from our attachments to this and that and begin searching for another way to make our life satisfying and meaningful

The whole philosophy of Buddhism in general and of tantra in particular is that, as human beings with virtually unlimited potential, we should aim for the highest pleasure possible. What true renunciation is based on is the realization that our ordinary pleasures are second rate. They are inconsequential when compared with the extraordinary bliss to be had from awakening the energies latent within us and fulfilling our deepest potential.
Instead of being uptight, from either craving after pleasure or rejecting it guiltily, we feel more at ease. Unpleasant circumstances cease to bother us so much.

This narrow concern for our own happiness and our own liberation makes it impossible for us to realize the vast potential of our human mind and heart. Such self-centered concern values the welfare of just one being — ourself — over the welfare of the countless others who share life’s problems with us.
Dedication simply means that, having created a certain atmosphere of positive energy within yourself, you determine to share this happiness with others as much as possible.
Self-cherishing is the cause of all misery and dissatisfaction, while holding all mother sentient beings dearer than oneself is the foundation of all realizations and knowledge.

The Panchen Lama goes on to suggest that we take a good look at what Shakyamuni Buddha did with his life. He gave up all his self-attachment, dedicated himself completely to the welfare of others, and as a result attained the unsurpassed bliss of complete enlightenment
If we are sincerely intent on achieving the highest human pleasure, therefore, we must give our mind space by developing an attitude of renunciation

In Buddhist terminology this supreme motivation is known as bodhichitta. It is the impulse to achieve full enlightenment (bodhi, or buddhahood) in order to be of the most benefit to others. Only through dedicating ourselves to working for the happiness of all beings — in other words only by cultivating the open heart of bodhichitta — can we ever experience supreme happiness ourselves.
When you have developed bodhichitta in your heart all the good things in life are magnetically attracted to you and effortlessly pour down upon you like rain.
This supremely compassionate outlook is a direct result of clear insight into our own essential reality and the reality of others

The only way to break free from this neurotic obsession with ourselves is by opening our hearts to others. When we are truly concerned with the welfare of someone else we automatically cease to be so concerned with our own problems, at least for a while.

It can be said that merely possessing this compassionate bodhichitta is a type of enlightened experience. As we create this open space in our consciousness, we take on a much more universal character.
The fact is, while we are cultivating love, compassion, wisdom, and all the other insights that lead to enlightenment, we can be helping others continuously

If you have a clear and simple understanding of the philosophy and psychology of bodhichitta and try to act accordingly in everyday life, experimenting with this open-hearted dedication to others in all your actions, that is a sufficient spiritual practice
Just as level ground is the basis on which you build a house, so too is equanimity — an unbiased attitude toward all other beings — the foundation for cultivating bodhichitta

And when you reflect that each living being has, over beginningless past lifetimes, done the same kind and unkind things to you as the friend and enemy of this life, you will come to see that all are equal in having been friend, enemy, and stranger to you over and over again
As a prerequisite for the successful practice of tantra, the development of bodhichitta is absolutely necessary.

They realize that the longer it takes them to achieve enlightenment, the longer everyone who needs help will have to wait. The lightning vehicle of tantra is therefore intended for those who wish to help others as much as possible, as quickly as possible

Now we will consider the third basic prerequisite: cultivation of the correct view.
In this context the correct view means the wisdom that clearly realizes the actual way in which we and all other phenomena exist.

But we can begin this process right now merely by being a bit skeptical about what appears to our mind. For example, as soon as we realize that we are holding on to a solid view of ourselves — “I am like this,” “I should be like that” — we should remember that this view is nothing but a fantasy, a momentary projection of our mind

Despite how real they seemed, these people in fact lack even an atom of self-existence. Completely empty of any objective existence whatsoever, they were only the hallucination of our dream experience.

The point is that the people and things that make up our sensory world do not exist in the solid, objective way that they now appear to us. These appearances are nothing but the manifestations of our ordinary consciousness; they are merely apprehended or labeled by our superstitious mind
We instinctively feel that we exist as something very real, definite, and substantial. We have no doubt about this real me and it seems absurd to think of it as just another hallucination

Our ego — in this context, the neurotic mind that grasps on to a solid sense of self-identity for support — is extremely powerful and will fight against any view that threatens its security. It is deeply disturbed by the suggestion that the “I,” like everything else, is something merely designated by conceptual thought
We and all other phenomena without exception are empty of even the smallest atom of self-existence, and it is this emptiness (shunyata) that is the ultimate nature of everything that exists.

In a similar way, all existent phenomena are mere appearances to the mind; lacking concrete self-existence, they come into being from the interplay of various causes and conditions. They arise, abide, and disappear, all the while constantly changing

From the Buddhist point of view, all the circumstances of our life are manifestations of our own consciousness. This is the central understanding of Buddhism. Painful and confusing situations derive from a painful and confused mind, and whatever happiness we experience — from ordinary pleasure to the highest realization of enlightenment — is also rooted in our own mind.

The only sensible approach is to train ourselves to observe our thoughts without following them. This deprives them of their compulsive energy and is therefore like removing the pot of boiling water from the fire
This constant changing of our likes and dislikes is another sign that our ordinary concrete concepts of reality are mistaken and nothing but the projections of a confused and superstitious mind
What we need to learn, then, is how to maintain clear awareness while cutting off our habitual reaction to things

Our mind constantly churns out all kinds of dualistic garbage like this and our life reflects the confusion. One result is that our relationships with people and things are fickle and unstable. First we are interested in a new friend; the next day we discard him.
The deep, peaceful clarity of our essential mind is in the nature of love, and in this calm atmosphere the disturbances of hatred and anger have no place.

Within this expanse of non-self-existent reality, all things function perfectly without obstructing one another. There is no conflict, no confusion, and no separation. Instead of feeling alienated from our environment, from others, or even from ourselves, we share in the experience of universal harmony

Without focusing on any object, merely gaze out into space with intensive awareness and let go of all ideas about yourself. You are there, the blue infinity of space is there, and nothing else appears. As we fill our consciousness with this experience of the clarity of space, we will naturally come to contemplate the clarity of our mind.

Tantra contains powerful methods for awakening the very subtlest level of mind and for directing this blissful, subtle, clear-light consciousness toward the spacious and penetrating vision of nonduality

From the tantric point of view, whenever we open our mind and senses to the objective world, our perception is always related to a particular color. And each color that we perceive — blue, red, green, and so on — is directly related to what is happening in our internal world. That is why in the practice of tantra, with its visualization of deities and so forth, color and light play such an important part.

The bliss that arises while contemplating the clarity of our consciousness is a powerful antidote to this restlessness. It has the ability to provide a calm and deep satisfaction unmatched by ordinary pleasures.

But beneath the gross levels at which these delusions function there is something more subtle, more basic to our nature. And it is this essential aspect of our human consciousness that has the potential of becoming fully awakened and everlastingly blissful

We have to realize that our low opinion of ourselves, which keeps us trapped in the cycle of perpetual dissatisfaction, only arises because we are ignorant of our basic, essentially pure nature. By generating the prerequisite renunciation, bodhichitta, and wisdom, and by delving into the clear nature of our mind, we create the space in which true self-transformation can take place.
Instead, we learn to identify our innermost mind with that of our guru, who is seen as inseparable from everyone who has already achieved complete awakening.

The guru’s energy of great compassion, great love, great wisdom, and great skill take seed in us so that we ourselves come to embody these limitlessly beneficial qualities. We ourselves become the guru and, as such, can give immeasurable and inexhaustible help to all beings. If we do not generate the qualities of a true guru within us, how can we provide ultimate benefit for anyone else?

Practically speaking, there is only so much the relative, external guru can do for us; he or she cannot guarantee that we gain insight and realizations. But our inner guru, our own clear wisdom, can accomplish everything. The practice of guru yoga, therefore, is primarily a method for learning how to listen to this inner guru.

For us to progress along the tantric path to complete self-fulfillment there must be a meeting of the inner and outer gurus. Our own enlightened potential must be energized and inspired by contact with someone who has already developed this potential to the full.

The strength of tantra — which has the literal meaning of “continuous” or “continuity” — lies in its preservation and transmission of the enlightened experience through a continuous, unbroken lineage of practitioners. Therefore, it is necessary that we establish contact with this vital lineage of transmission if we wish to transform ourselves, and the way this contact is made is through initiation, or empowerment.
Naropa’s mind was so magnetized by this unorthodox initiation that he immediately entered into a deep and blissful state of meditative absorption (samadhi)

It is a special kind of communication between guru and disciple and therefore depends as much upon the disciple’s openness and level of development as it does on the guru’s realizations. This intimate communication activates our inner nature in such a way that we are empowered to practice uninterruptedly and complete all the attainments along the path to self-fulfillment.

True empowerment only occurs when there is active participation by both the disciple and the teacher. It is an act of two consciousnesses sharing the same experience. Only when this happens can it truly be said that empowerment has taken place.

Merely to imagine an experience plants seeds in the vast field of your consciousness and eventually these seeds will ripen into the actual experience itself. This is a natural progression. So you should always remain open and relaxed and be satisfied with whatever happens.

The essence of the guru is wisdom: the perfectly clear and radiant state of mind in which bliss and the realization of emptiness are inseparably unified. Therefore, when we visualize the guru absorbing into our heart we should feel that an indestructible impression of that wisdom is being made upon our fundamental mind

By visualizing in this way and thinking of the personal kindness shown to you by your guru, a powerful connection is established. Instead of being some vague, impersonal image, the deity is seen as being inseparable in essence from your own immeasurably kind spiritual guide
Your visualization magnetically attracts such inspiration, such blessing, and this enables you to develop clear realizations. This, after all, is the entire point of the guru yoga practice

Seeing the underlying unity of our guru, the deity, and ourselves is not something we do only during formal meditational practice. We need to practice guru yoga — identifying ourselves with the guru’s essential buddha nature — during every moment of our life
We must become intimately familiar with the essential oneness of the guru, the deity, and our own innermost nature
manifests in the three

That is the fundamental concern of tantra. When you develop yourself fully so that your entire inner potential is realized, then you yourself become a deity, you yourself become a buddha. This is the ultimate aim of guru yoga.

Despite the fact that spiritual understanding is meant to soften our concrete, limiting preconceptions and subdue our delusions, it is nevertheless possible to contain a lot of intellectual knowledge about religion while remaining unchanged by it. A dry, intellectual approach to spiritual matters leaves our heart untouched and unaffected.

As we have discussed, it is the guru who provides this necessary inspiration, this link between our consciousness and the actual experience of transcendence. In the behavior of our own guru we can see for ourselves the beneficial effects of training the mind in love and wisdom

While engaged in the practices of guru devotion we should be patient and proceed gradually. It is extremely important not to force ourselves, to do what does not feel right out of some misplaced sense of obligation; I am thinking particularly of the practice of seeing the guru as inseparable from the meditational deity.
That is why we have to train again and again in those visualization practices that dissolve our false notion of concrete self-existence and strengthen our understanding and experience of nonduality

If you have not yet tasted the bliss of your fundamental mind, and have not seen for yourself how you can achieve a state of penetrative awareness and openness far surpassing what you now feel is possible, naturally you will be very skeptical.

But within the boundaries, or atmosphere, of this body is another, far more subtle, body: the so-called vajra body, “vajra” having the connotation of indestructible. Just as our gross and perishable physical body is pervaded by the ordinary nervous system, this subtle vajra body is pervaded by thousands of channels (nadi) through which flow the energy winds (prana) and drops (bindu) that are the source of the bliss so vital to highest tantric practice.
Once we have made contact with this clear, conscious body of light through meditation, our gross physical body will no longer be a problem for us, for we will have transcended it
The most important chakra, however, is the one located at the level of the heart, for the heart chakra is the home of our very subtle mind: the priceless treasure of all tantric practitioners.

The dissolution of our vajra body’s energy winds into the central channel is crucial to advanced tantric practice, and because this dissolution takes place naturally when we die we should become as familiar as possible now with the process of death.

What we have to realize, therefore, is that death is not a sudden and terrifying annihilation but a gradual process during which our mind grows more and more fine and subtle. If we want to practice highest tantra, or even if we merely want to prepare for what we must all eventually encounter, we should become as familiar with this gradual process as we can now. If we wait until the moment of death itself, it will be too late.

When all the veils currently obscuring our mind have been removed and when all of our positive potentials have been developed to their utmost, there is the simultaneous achievement of the truth body (dharmakaya), enjoyment body (sambhogakaya), and emanation body (nirmanakaya) of a buddha.
If we neglect to use our body’s precious energy for the attainment of enlightenment, and squander it instead on the meaningless pursuits of this life, then we are far more ignorant than those farmers

and so forth — and who also know how to put this energy to constructive use. In other words, we should be skillful, and the highest skill involves transforming our present body from a source of pain and dissatisfaction into the blissful path to unsurpassed happiness for ourselves and others. This is the ultimate goal of all tantric practice.

remaining caught up in intellectual preconceptions can prevent us from entering profound meditational experiences. So it is important to know when to relax, let go, and allow the mind to settle into its natural state of clarity.

To avoid this confusion we should realize that “cutting rebirth” has a very specific meaning: namely, to free ourselves from having to experience uncontrolled rebirth again and again
So those people who get something really clear in their mind and then, the minute they understand it, put it directly into their heart — these are the people who are truly practicing.

Tantra says that human beings have a truly divine quality. The nucleus of each human being, each person’s essential nature, is something divine, something pure. To realize this, and to make this realization an integral part of our life and not a mere intellectualization, it is necessary, as we have already discussed, to emanate strongly as a deity.

To gain the true emptiness experience you have to begin somewhere. You have to have some experience, some taste of what it is like to go beyond the mundane, ego-generated puzzles of this and that. This is the main point. Somehow we have to let go of all the gross, concrete, and limiting concepts keeping us trapped in an unsatisfactory, mundane view of ourselves and everything else.

When you see yourself as a deity, you should feel that you are the real emanation of the deity. Don’t think that you are just pretending; you should be convinced. Then, like the actor who remains in character even after the play is finished, you might surprise yourself to find that you have actually become the deity. Such divine pride — the strong sense of actually being the deity — is crucial.

The essence of tantra is dealing skillfully with pleasure. The person who qualifies for tantra is someone who can cope with pleasure, someone for whom dealing with pleasure becomes a conducive situation for achieving liberation.
The purpose of generating ourselves as a deity through the practice of the three bodies, or kayas, of a buddha is to smash through our self-pitying concept, our suffocating conception of ego
This does not mean we should not have pleasure. We should have pleasure, but we need to keep from going out of control while experiencing pleasure.

First of all, although tummo practice definitely leads to the experience of bliss, its primary purpose is to enable us to enter into a state of clear-light wisdom

What are dakas and dakinis? Simply speaking, they are males and females who possess advanced experiences of tantric transformation and control and are therefore able to increase the blissful wisdom of a highly qualified practitioner.

When you enter into any meditational practice, no matter how difficult it may appear at first, you should try to be brave and think, “Whether I am completely successful or not, at least I’ll try to gain some experience.” Do not feel, “How can I meditate? I’m new to this and know nothing about meditation.

Also, I have noticed that the people who have created heavy negativities in their lives are often the most successful when they turn to spiritual matters,

My point in mentioning all this is that, as a human being, you should never set a limit on how much you can accomplish, no matter what your life has been like so far. It could be that your attempts at meditation have been full of distraction, and suddenly some potential ripens, giving you the surprising ability to concentrate uninterruptedly for long periods of time

Lastly, if we wish to attain the highest realization we should keep our practices hidden. This may sound peculiar but it is actually a very important point. In fact, the correct term for the practice of tantra is “secret mantra.” Here, “mantra” means protection of the mind and “secret” is a reminder that these powerful methods should be kept to ourselves, like a precious treasure.
It is far better to retain a subdued outer appearance and be a great yogi inwardly than it is to make a big show on the outside but have no realizations within.

What stopped me specifically, reading the Shiva Purana for the first time in the version that a colleague had pressed on me with the specific enthusiasm of the recently converted, was a particular passage in the Vayaviya Samhita in which Shiva is described simultaneously as the absolute, attributeless ground of all being—the Nishkala whose nature is pure consciousness without quality or differentiation—and as the fully personal, fully present shepherd of every individual soul, the one who knows each Pashu by name, who has been walking alongside each one since before time began, and who will not cease walking alongside until the last one has recognized what it is.

Within the first few verses of the Vidyeshvara Samhita, its opening book, it announces something extraordinary: that it is the greatest of all the Puranas, that the god it describes is the supreme reality, and that merely hearing it confers liberation. The text does not argue for its authority. It simply states it, as if authority were a given—as if the very act of beginning were itself proof enough.

In the Sanskrit intellectual tradition, the Puranas were not simply old stories. They were a recognized category of sacred literature—one of the primary vehicles through which the vast, complex, and sometimes mutually contradictory body of Hindu thought was transmitted to the general population across the centuries.

Each Purana, according to classical definition, was supposed to contain five defining characteristics—the Panchalakshana (पञ्चलक्षण, pañcalakṣaṇa): cosmogony, secondary creation after dissolution, the genealogy of the gods, the reigns of the Manus, and the histories of the solar and lunar dynasties.

What the text actually wants to do—what it is burning to do—is to argue, at every level and through every available literary form, that Shiva is the supreme reality and that knowledge of Shiva is the ultimate human attainment.

Sadashiva is not this. Or rather—Sadashiva is not only this. The Shiva Purana's central theological claim, developed across all seven of its Samhitas with extraordinary philosophical sophistication, is that Shiva is simultaneously the personal deity who dances on Mount Kailash, who falls in love with Parvati, who burns Kama to ash with his third eye, who swallows poison to save the universe—and the impersonal, infinite, beginningless, endless ground of all being from which the entire universe, including all the other gods, arises and into which it periodically returns.

The Samhita's account of Sadashiva begins with what is philosophically the most fundamental claim: that Sadashiva is Nirguna (निर्गुण, nirguṇa)—without qualities, without attributes, beyond all characterization. This immediately puts the Shiva Purana in conversation with one of the central debates in Indian philosophy: the debate between the Nirguna Brahman of Advaita Vedanta and the Saguna Brahman (the divine with qualities) of the theistic schools.

The universe is not separate from him—not an artifact standing outside its maker—but a continuous, ongoing expression of his nature. The Sanskrit term for this relationship is Abhinna (अभिन्न, abhinna)—non-separation or non-difference. The universe is Abhinna from Sadashiva in the sense that a wave is non-different from the ocean: it has a distinct form, a distinct identity that can be perceived and named and measured, but it has no existence apart from the water.
In the same way, the universe is real—the Shiva Purana is not Advaita in the sense of denying the reality of multiplicity—but its multiplicity does not constitute a reality separate from Sadashiva.

But the foundation of that answer is laid here, in the doctrine of Sadashiva: every individual soul—every Jiva (जीव, jīva)—is, at its deepest level, a point of Sadashiva's own self-awareness. Not identical to Sadashiva in the way that would erase individuality, but not separate from him in the way that would make liberation a journey across an unbridgeable ontological gulf. The Jiva is, as the Shiva Purana puts it in a phrase of great precision, Shiva-svarupa (शिवस्वरूप, śivasvarūpa)—of the very nature of Shiva—though obscured from the recognition of this by the conditioning forces of Maya and karma.

The Shiva Purana's metaphysics of Shakti begins with a claim that initially sounds paradoxical: Shakti is not separate from Shiva. She is his own power, his own dynamic nature, as inseparable from him as heat is from fire or brightness from the sun. A fire without heat is not a diminished fire—it is simply not a fire at all. Similarly, Sadashiva without Shakti is not Sadashiva at a lower level of functioning.

Together they constitute a complete account not only of cosmic history but of the structure of every individual soul's relationship to Sadashiva—for the Shiva Purana teaches that these five acts are not only cosmic events occurring on the scale of universes and aeons but are simultaneously occurring in every individual consciousness in every moment.

The analogy used repeatedly in the text is sleep: just as a person who falls into deep sleep does not cease to exist but returns to an undifferentiated state from which they will re-emerge refreshed and renewed, the universe in dissolution returns to Sadashiva not as a death but as a rest, a reabsorption into the infinite that will be followed, in due course, by a new Srishti.

Tirobhava operates at the level of individual consciousness—it is the act by which Sadashiva appears to forget himself in each finite soul, the act that makes limited individual experience possible and that generates the three Malas.

Anugraha (अनुग्रह, anugraha)—grace, favor, the lifting of the veil—is the fifth and, from the soteriological perspective, the most important of Shiva's five acts. Anugraha is the act by which Sadashiva removes the concealment he himself imposed, restores the soul's recognition of its own divine nature, and brings the entire arc of Tirobhava to its inevitable and joyful conclusion.

What does it actually look like—experientially, psychologically, spiritually—when Anugraha begins to operate in an individual soul? The Shiva Purana addresses this question across multiple Samhitas, and its answers are more precise and more phenomenologically rich than is sometimes recognized. The text is not simply describing an abstract process of cosmic realignment. It is describing something that happens in consciousness—a progressive shift in how the world is perceived, how the self is understood, and how the relationship between the individual and the infinite is experienced.

In the Shaiva context, Jnana does not mean the acquisition of new intellectual information. It means a direct, unmediated recognition—the Sanskrit word that most precisely captures it is Pratyabhijna (प्रत्यभिज्ञा, pratyabhijñā), which means "re-cognition" in the most literal sense: not the knowing of something for the first time but the re-knowing, the remembering, the recognizing of what was always already known but temporarily forgotten.

Liberation in the Shiva Purana is not the soul arriving somewhere it has never been before. It is the soul recognizing where it has always been. This recognition does not, according to the Shiva Purana, necessarily arrive as a sudden dramatic illumination—though it can. More commonly, it arrives as a progressive deepening of the quality of awareness, a gradual thinning of the veils of the three Malas, a growing transparency of individual consciousness to the infinite consciousness that underlies it.

Sadashiva does not become more Sadashiva as a result of the soul's liberation. The soul becomes more capable of recognizing what Sadashiva has always been—and what it has always, at its deepest level, been itself.

Liberation is not merely the dissolution of the individual into the impersonal Absolute. It is the fulfillment of the individual's relationship with Shiva. The liberated soul does not cease to be a soul—it does not lose its capacity for love, for devotion, for the specific quality of awareness that constitutes its unique perspective. What it loses is the Mala-driven sense of separation that made love feel like a reaching toward something absent.

This has practical implications that the Shiva Purana draws out explicitly. If Sadashiva is the innermost reality of all beings—not just of Shaiva devotees, not just of human beings, not just of living beings, but of all that exists—then the way one treats the world is inseparable from the way one relates to Shiva.

The Shiva Purana's account of Sadashiva is, at its deepest level, an account of a love story. Not a love story in the ordinary sense—not the story of two beings who find each other across the distance of separation—but something stranger and more beautiful: the story of a single infinite consciousness that loves itself so completely that it is willing to forget itself in order to experience the joy of recognition. Every individual soul, in this telling, is Shiva playing at being other than Shiva. Every moment of genuine spiritual longing—every ache for something beyond the ordinary, every glimpse of beauty or meaning that feels larger than its occasion—is Shiva beginning to remember. And the liberation that the Shiva Purana promises is not a reward for spiritual achievement. It is an inevitability. Because the ocean cannot permanently fail to recognize itself in the wave. Because infinite consciousness, however deeply it has played at being finite, carries within it—always, ineradicably—the seed of its own recognition. The Sanskrit word for this seed is Shiva himself. He is both the seeker and what is sought. He is both the question and the only answer that does not produce another question.

Shiva's self-manifestation is not concentrated at a single sacred center but is spread across the entire land, making the subcontinent as a whole into a kind of living Linga, a place where the infinite is perpetually available to those who know how to approach it.

The theology underlying Pratishtha is rich and philosophically serious. It is not magic in any primitive sense—not the compulsion of a divine being by ritual means. It is, rather, an application of the Shiva Purana's understanding of Anugraha: the recognition that Sadashiva is already everywhere, that his presence does not need to be created because it is already the innermost reality of every location and every object, and that the function of the consecration ritual is not to bring Shiva into the Linga but to establish the conditions under which devotees can reliably and repeatedly access a presence that is already there.

This is the methodological failure at the heart of the misreading, and it is a failure of a kind that has been systematically identified and critiqued in the philosophy of the social sciences—what the anthropologist Clifford Geertz called the failure of "thick description," the reduction of a culturally embedded practice to its thinnest possible description stripped of all the meanings that make it what it is for its practitioners.

The pillar is consciousness. The pillar is the Absolute. The pillar is that which supports all things while being supported by nothing. This is precisely the theology of the Jyotirlinga: the pillar of infinite light that has no base and no summit, that supports all creation while being supported by nothing outside itself.

In the yogic tradition, the upward movement of sexual energy through the practice of brahmacharya—celibacy—is associated with the acquisition of extraordinary spiritual power, the ojas or spiritual radiance that accumulates when biological energy is redirected toward consciousness.

The most philosophically interesting of these accounts is the identification of the three leaflets of the Bilva with the three Malas—the three impurities that bind the individual soul to the cycle of finite experience. When the devotee offers Bilva leaves to Shiva, the offering is understood as a gesture of surrendering the three Malas to the divine—an acknowledgment that the bonds of Anavamala, Mayiyamala, and Karmamala are not the ultimate truth of one's being, and a request for the Anugraha that will progressively dissolve them.

The ash of the cremation ground is what remains after everything transient has been burned away: the body, the ego, the accumulated identification with what is finite and impermanent. What remains is not nothing. It is the irreducible residue, the proof that something cannot be destroyed, the mark of the indestructible ground of being that Shiva himself is.
The directional association of Ya is all-encompassing—space is the field within which all the other elements exist—and its associated deity is Sadashiva himself in his most complete self-revelation.
Om is the mantra at the level of Nishkala Shiva—the formless, attributeless absolute. Na-Ma-Shi-Va-Ya is the mantra at the level of Sakala Shiva—the formed, qualified, accessible personal deity.

This relationship between Om and the Panchakshara has practical implications for how the mantra is recited. The tradition distinguishes between the Saguna recitation—the outward, audible sounding of the syllables in the Vaikhari mode—and the Nirguna recitation—the interior, silent holding of the mantra at the level of Para-Vak, the level at which sound and consciousness are identical.

Ajapa-Japa is not a technique that the practitioner performs. It is a recognition that the practitioner receives—the recognition that the universe has been reciting Namashivaya from the beginning, that every breath is a sounding of the mantra, that the five elements which constitute the physical world are the Panchakshara in material form.

the Panchakshara is not a mantra that can be taken up independently, studied from a book, and practiced alone without initiation. The text insists, with a regularity that suggests it is responding to a real tendency it observes in its audience, that the mantra must be received from a qualified teacher—a Guru—who has himself received it in an unbroken lineage of transmission stretching back, in principle, to its original revelation by Shiva himself.

is like the transmission of fire, which requires contact with an already burning flame. A printed description of fire does not ignite. A description of the Panchakshara does not activate the mantra's living quality. What activates it is the transmission of vibrational recognition from a consciousness in which the mantra is already alive to a consciousness that is prepared to receive it.

Through Diksha, several things happen simultaneously. The Guru transmits the mantra in its living form. The disciple's Malas—the three impurities discussed in Chapter Two—are partially attenuated by the power of the initiation, creating the conditions under which the mantra's practice will be most effective.

The modern seeker who approaches the Panchakshara with genuine Shraddha, with philosophical understanding, with sincere devotion, and with a willingness to seek qualified guidance when it becomes available is not outside the tradition's understanding of who the mantra is for. The Shiva Purana's most consistent message, across all seven of its Samhitas, is that the door to Shiva is always open. The question is always about the quality of attention we bring to it.

The Shiva Purana tells stories—some of its most beloved stories—of people whose Panchakshara practice transformed their lives and ultimately liberated them despite having no formal theological training, no Sanskrit, no access to a qualified teacher. The mantra works. Even when the practitioner does not fully know how.

Shiva responds to Shraddha. The quality of attention and the sincerity of the heart are the conditions the divine actually requires. Everything else—the correct pronunciation, the philosophical understanding, the proper ritual procedure—are refinements that deepen and accelerate a process that can begin wherever genuine devotion is found.

Upamshu Japa (उपांशु जप, upāṃśu japa) is murmured or whispered recitation—the mantra formed by the lips and tongue without full vocalization, audible only to oneself. This mode is understood to be ten times more powerful than audible recitation, because the withdrawal of the mantra from full external expression begins the process of internalization—the movement of the mantra's vibration from the Vaikhari toward the Madhyama level.

The Mala itself has a specific structure that reflects the theology of Shiva's relationship to his devotees. The 108 regular beads are interrupted by a single larger bead—the Sumeru or the Meru bead—which is never crossed during counting.

The practitioner who never crosses the Meru is acknowledging, in every round of practice, that Shiva is not one bead among many—not one recitation among many recitations—but the ground that makes all recitation possible and the destination toward which all recitation moves.

The text goes so far as to say that even an inadvertent utterance of Namashivaya—even saying the syllables by accident, without devotional intent—generates spiritual merit. And it explicitly states that Shiva's name, once genuinely received into the heart, begins a process of purification that the practitioner cannot stop even if she wanted to.

The remedy for Namaparadha, the Shiva Purana says, is more of the name itself—but approached with greater humility, greater honesty, and a clearer understanding of what the name is and what it is for. This is one of the most psychologically wise passages in the entire Purana.

The divine name is simultaneously the wound and the medicine, the problem and its resolution—because all genuine spiritual problems, in the Shiva Purana's understanding, are ultimately variations of the same problem: the failure to recognize Sadashiva, which is the Tirobhava function operating at full strength.

When Manikkavacakar writes that the five letters are the raft on which the drowning soul crosses the ocean of birth and death, he is not deploying a metaphor. He is reporting an experience. The Panchakshara kept him alive in the darkest passages of his spiritual journey, not as a philosophical map but as a rope—something to hold onto when the intellectual understanding had dissolved and only the bare practice remained.

This is a crucial point. Brahma does not create the world from nothing or from pure creative fancy. He creates it from the accumulated karmic heritage of all the beings whose tendencies and unresolved experiences persisted through the great dissolution. The specific form the world takes in any given cosmic cycle is, in this sense, the precise form required to allow those beings to continue their journey—to work through the karma they brought with them from the previous cycle, to develop what they need to develop, to eventually recognize what they are.

At the highest level of the hierarchy are the Devas (देव, deva)—the divine beings, often translated as gods, who inhabit the luminous upper realms of the fourteen-world cosmological scheme. The Devas are not gods in the Western monotheistic sense of independently existing supernatural beings with inherent divine status. They are, in the Shiva Purana's understanding, souls who have accumulated through many lifetimes of virtuous action and spiritual practice the level of refined consciousness that allows them to function at these elevated levels of reality. They possess extraordinary powers—the Siddhis (सिद्धि, siddhi) that the tradition describes in considerable detail—and they experience the realms they inhabit as states of consciousness qualitatively different from and subtler than ordinary human experience.

The Shiva Purana is consistent in its insistence that even the most exalted Deva—even Brahma, even Vishnu, even Indra the king of the gods—is not beyond the need for liberation, and that liberation is available only through Shiva's grace, not through the accumulation of divine merit alone.

Below the Devas in the hierarchy are the human beings—the Manushyas (मनुष्य, manuṣya)—and here the Srishti Khanda makes a claim that has been misunderstood as arrogance but is actually a precise soteriological observation: that the human state, while lower than the divine states in terms of power and refinement of experience, is uniquely precious because it is the level at which the possibility of liberation is most accessible.

The Guna of Rajas is not simply an obstacle to be overcome. The tradition recognizes that Rajasic energy, properly directed, is the fuel of spiritual practice. The drive and determination required to sustain a genuine contemplative life—to maintain daily Japa, to study difficult philosophical texts, to engage seriously with the practice of self-inquiry—are Rajasic energies harnessed in service of Sattvic ends.

The grace-function exists because suffering is real and because the real suffering of real beings is something that the infinite consciousness at the heart of reality does not simply watch from a position of cosmic detachment.

Irenaeus's "soul-making" account, holds that a world in which liberation is possible must be a world in which the contrast between bondage and freedom is real—a world in which the soul can genuinely not know what it is, can genuinely suffer from that not-knowing, and can genuinely move toward the recognition that transforms suffering into joy.

What the text does offer, ultimately, is not a logical proof that suffering is justified but an experiential claim: that the soul which has moved through suffering into the recognition of its own nature as Shiva-svarupa does not look back on its suffering as an injustice or an error. It looks back on it the way a long illness is sometimes retrospectively experienced after genuine recovery—not as something good in itself, but as the specific journey that led to the specific health that could not have been reached any other way.

The Shiva Purana's answer is given with a simplicity that, after the complexity of the cosmological narrative that precedes it, carries something of the force of the obvious: the universe exists for liberation. Not in the sense that liberation is the only thing that happens in the universe—countless other things happen, of enormous variety and richness—but in the sense that liberation is the direction in which the entire structure of the universe is oriented, the destination toward which every soul in every realm is, at whatever speed and by whatever route their karma allows, inevitably moving.

highlights.text: The Shiva Purana uses a striking phrase to describe this soteriological structure of the cosmos: it calls the universe Shiva's Karuna (करुणा, karuṇā)—his compassion. The universe is not a test, not a punishment, not an entertainment, not a philosophical thought-experiment conducted by an abstract absolute. It is an act of compassion.

It is the specific structure that Sadashiva's infinite compassion has produced in order to give every bound soul—every Pasha-bound Pashu (पाशुपत पशु, pāśu) in the Shaiva terminology, every individual consciousness caught in the net of the three Malas—the precise experiential environment it needs to work through its karma, develop its capacity for recognition, and eventually receive the grace that liberates it.

What it does is situate all of it within a larger context of meaning that the suffering itself cannot provide but that the tradition's vision of the whole can: every soul, however deep in the darkness of Tamasic contraction, however thoroughly bound by the three Malas, is being held—actively, compassionately, patiently held—within the creative consciousness of the same Sadashiva who whispers the Panchakshara at the moment of death in Kashi.

mythology is not a lesser form of knowledge than philosophy. It is a different mode of the same knowledge, operating through different faculties and reaching dimensions of truth that philosophical argument, for all its precision, cannot adequately capture.
And this choice—this act of total, unconditional devotion in the face of social disapproval—is itself a theological statement before a single dramatic event of the Sati Khanda has occurred.

This is theologically significant because it means that Sati's love for Shiva is not the love of an infinite being for itself. It is the love of an apparently finite being for what it recognizes, in the depths of its heart, as the ground of its own being—the love of the soul for Sadashiva, experienced from within the specific conditions of human finitude.

This mode of death is called Yogagni Marana (योगाग्नि मरण, yogāgni maraṇa)—death by the fire of yoga—and it is understood in the Shaiva tradition not as suicide in any ordinary psychological sense but as the deliberate withdrawal of Shakti from a form that has been rendered uninhabitable by the defilement of the insult to Shiva.

He is born from it—torn from one of Shiva's own matted locks and flung into being as a warrior of terrifying power, a being whose entire existence is the expression of a single aspect of Sadashiva's nature: the aspect of righteous wrath at the desecration of what is sacred.

It is auspicious violence—the violence that restores the sacred order that has been violated, the destruction that is ultimately in service of what the Shiva Purana calls Dharma (धर्म, dharma), the proper order of things.

A goat is an animal that eats indiscriminately, that cannot distinguish between what is nutritious and what is not, that follows appetite without discrimination. Daksha's replacement head is the tradition's iconographic commentary on the theological failure that led to his destruction: the failure to distinguish between genuine divine presence and institutional convention, between the wild god who is the ground of being and the domesticated divinity that institutional religion is comfortable with.

The pilgrim who visits a Shaktipeeth is visiting a place where the goddess is particularly and powerfully present, where the accumulated devotion of generations of pilgrims has reinforced and deepened the original sacred charge of the site.

When a piece of Sati's body falls and becomes sacred, what is being described is not merely a local increase in divine energy at that spot. It is the permanent inscription of the goddess's presence into the substance of the land itself.

Each piece of the body carries the full quality of Sati's Shakti—not a fraction of it, but the whole of it expressed through a specific aspect. The breast that falls at Kamakhya carries the fullness of Shakti's creative and erotic power. The eyes that fall at Naina Devi carry the fullness of her witnessing consciousness. The different pieces are not portions of a divided whole. They are complete expressions of different dimensions of the same infinite whole.

The pilgrim who travels through India is not merely traveling through a country that happens to contain sacred sites. She is traveling through the body of the goddess herself, and every step she takes on this land is a step taken on sacred ground. "When Sati's body was divided, Shiva did not lose her. He found her everywhere. Every piece that fell became a meeting place. Every place of her falling became a place of his presence. This is the deepest meaning of the Shaktipeethas: that loss, when it is total enough, becomes a kind of omnipresence."—Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Sati Khanda 20.31

The tradition distilled from the Sati Khanda's theology is sometimes called Jnana-Bhakti Yoga—the path of devoted knowledge—and its central insistence is precisely this: that devotion without understanding is blind, and that understanding without devotion is hollow, but that the two together constitute the only religious practice that can remain genuinely open to the divine in whatever form it chooses to appear.

The wild ascetic, the frequenter of cremation grounds, the god who wears skulls and consorts with outcasts—this is not what the institutional religious imagination of Daksha's world recognizes as the supreme deity. And so it excludes him. The theological point the Shiva Purana is making is not merely that this particular exclusion was mistaken—that Shiva happened to be the supreme deity and therefore should have been invited. It is making the more general and more challenging claim that genuine religious life must remain permanently open to the divine in forms that the institutional imagination does not recognize and cannot domesticate.

The Shiva Purana's movement from Sati to Parvati is therefore a movement from the devotion of recognition—the love of a soul that already knows, at some pre-reflective level, what it loves—to the devotion of seeking—the love of a soul that does not yet possess what it loves and must pursue it through every obstacle that the universe places in the path.

But the Parvati Khanda, which we enter in the next chapter, is in certain respects the more complete account of what devotion actually demands of the human soul—because most souls are not born with Sati's spontaneous recognition of the divine. Most souls must seek. Most souls must practice. Most souls must endure the long uncertainty of not knowing whether what they are reaching toward is real, and whether what they have given up for it was worth the giving. Parvati's story is their story.

"She did not wait for Shiva to choose her. She chose him, and then she made herself into someone he could not refuse. This is the oldest teaching in the Parvati Khanda: that longing is not passive, and that the divine responds not to those who wait but to those who burn."

That quietness is deliberate. The Parvati Khanda is the Shiva Purana's most carefully constructed narrative of how genuine spiritual pursuit actually begins—not in dramatic revelation or cosmic appointment, but in something much more ordinary and much more mysterious: the arising, in a specific consciousness, of a longing that has no satisfactory worldly object.

The story is useful precisely because it begins where most genuine spiritual lives begin: not with certainty, not with a clear destination, but with an orientation—a persistent sense that there is something worth everything, even if the precise shape of that something is not yet clear.

the people who most oppose the spiritual seeker's pursuit are often not the indifferent or the hostile but the loving—those whose love is real but whose frame of reference cannot contain what the seeker has committed to. This opposition is not an obstacle to be defeated. It is part of the price, and the tradition does not pretend it is cheap. "Mena said: Give up this madness. You are beautiful and you are royal and the world is full of worthy men. Why do you pursue this ash-smeared wanderer who cannot be domesticated, whose very nature resists the life I want for you? And Parvati said: Because everything you are offering me, I have already looked at carefully, and it is not what I want."—Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda 4.17

The word Tapas comes from the Sanskrit root tap, meaning to heat, to burn, to generate warmth. A fire burns. A fever burns. The sun burns. What each of these shares is the quality of concentrated, sustained, transformative energy—energy that does not merely pass through what it touches but changes it at the level of its structure. The fire does not merely warm the wood. It transforms wood into ash, releasing in the process the energy that was latent in the wood's structure. This is what the tradition means by Tapas as a spiritual practice: not pain as a value in itself, but the concentrated application of sustained will to the purification of consciousness—the burning away of everything in the practitioner's psychic structure that obstructs the recognition of what she is.

The Shiva Purana distinguishes, in its treatment of Parvati's practice, between three dimensions of Tapas that operate simultaneously. Kayika Tapas (कायिक तपस्, kāyika tapas) is the Tapas of the body—the physical disciplines that bring the gross instrument of the practitioner's action into alignment with her deepest intention. Vachika Tapas (वाचिक तपस्, vācika tapas) is the Tapas of speech—the discipline of using language only in ways that serve the recognition of truth, refusing the endless verbal elaboration of the ego's concerns that ordinarily occupies most of the mind's bandwidth. And Manasika Tapas (मानसिक तपस्, mānasika tapas) is the Tapas of the mind—the deepest and most demanding of the three, the practice of holding the mind's attention fixed on its object through every distraction, fatigue, and failure of motivation that the practice will inevitably encounter. The third form is the one the Shiva Purana regards as most significant, because it is the only one that actually changes the structure of consciousness rather than merely the condition of the body or the habits of speech. And it is the one that Parvati's narrative makes most visible.

The first stage of Parvati's tapas is described as Niyama-based practice—the establishment of a regular discipline of ritual purity, mantra recitation, and meditation at fixed times in a designated space.

This first stage is the stage most practitioners recognize from their own experience: the phase of initial enthusiasm, when the practice is new enough to sustain itself on novelty and the framework of the discipline is still providing enough structure to compensate for the as-yet undeveloped inner motivation. It is a necessary stage.

The transition to the second stage is precipitated not by success but by the encounter with futility. The narrative describes a point at which Parvati's regular practice has produced genuine refinement of consciousness—she is clearly more concentrated, more serene, more aligned with her deepest intention than when she began—but in which the specific object of her longing, Shiva himself, seems no closer.

The second stage is characterized by a dramatic intensification of physical austerity. Parvati moves deeper into the wilderness. She stops eating cooked food, then any food at all, sustaining herself eventually on fallen leaves—hence one of her epithets, Aparna (अपर्णा, aparṇā), the one without leaves, the one who eventually gives up even this minimal sustenance.

What the Shiva Purana is describing here is not self-punishment. It is the systematic dismantling of the ego's primary strategies for maintaining comfort and predictability—strategies that are, in the tradition's analysis, the same strategies that maintain the soul's comfortable distance from genuine recognition of its own nature. The body's demands for warmth, food, and protection from extremity are not bad in themselves.

The more theologically precise account—and the one that the Parvati Khanda's narrative actually supports—is that the delay is not a function of Shiva's withholding but of Parvati's progressive readiness. The divine is always present. What changes through the practice is the practitioner's capacity to receive that presence—what the tradition describes, in its philosophical language, as the progressive attenuation of the Malas. Each stage of Parvati's practice thins the veil between her consciousness and the recognition of what was always already available. The tapas does not earn Shiva's presence. It removes what was preventing the experience of a presence that was never actually absent.

What the extended tapas progressively accomplishes is the transformation of that wanting into something different: not the extinguishing of the orientation but the purification of it, the burning away of the ego's investment in the outcome until what remains is pure direction, pure attending, the Vairagya that has become so complete that even the goal has been released.

When Shiva finally appears in the Parvati Khanda, he does not appear as himself. He arrives in the form of a young Brahmin student—well-spoken, conventionally handsome, entirely recognizable as the kind of suitor Mena would have approved of—and he begins by doing the last thing Parvati expects: he speaks ill of Shiva.

What she does is defend Shiva with a precision and a passion that is itself the final demonstration of the readiness her tapas has produced. She does not become angry at the Brahmin student's words—or rather, she becomes angry, but her anger is entirely in service of clarity rather than in service of ego.

The young Brahmin student was not testing whether Parvati would fail or succeed. He was testing whether her recognition of Shiva was genuinely hers—whether it was rooted in the deep soil of her own transformation—or whether it was a borrowed conviction that would collapse under pressure.

He arrives attended by the gods, in a form that the Shiva Purana describes with deliberate emphasis as magnificent rather than transgressive—Nandikeshvara and the other divine attendants in their most resplendent aspect. This is Shiva choosing to make himself legible to a father's conventional love, choosing to meet the world of human concern at its own level rather than remaining entirely in the register of the transcendent.

Himavan's eventual consent is not the capitulation of a weaker will to a stronger one. It is saying, in effect, that there are dimensions of the divine nature that are accessible only through the specific mode of knowing that Parvati represents: the knowing that arises from the experience of finite love, from the willingness to be vulnerable, from the particular quality of consciousness that sustained devotional longing produces in a being who has gone through what Parvati has gone through.

The current cycle of Creation began around the year 36,000 B.C.E. In the beginning there was nothing more than a watery mass, a primeval ocean, called Nun. Nun is the body of Khepri. Prior to the creation, Khepri remained in a recumbent posture. He rested on the back of the great serpent Asha-hrau (“many faces”). From that Nun the Divine Spirit arose by stimulating Asha-hrau to move and churn the ocean. Then he named himself Khepri, Creator. Khepri called out his own name and  dchn –vibrations were infused in the ocean and waves vere formed. Just as there are many waves in the ocean with many shapes and sizes, the objects of the world came into being in the form of elements, Ra (fire), Shu (air-space), Tefnut (water), Geb (earth), Nut (ether). Everything in creation emanates from the Nun or primordial ocean, and expresses in the form of elements in succeeding levels of denseness. These elements also manifest in the form of the opposites of Creation (man-woman, up-down, white-black) which appear to be exclusive and separate from each other, but which are in reality complements to each other.

Khepri congealed the Nun, his own body, into all the forms of Creation. The first spot that was congealed from the Nun is called  Benben, the first place, the Ben-Ben dot, ·, of Creation. That dot is the center point in the symbol of Khepr-Ra $. That dot is the very point at the top of the Pyramid  mr- Obelisk,   tekhnu. The pyramid-obelisk symbolizes the mound that formed from that initial spot. Khepri sat atop the hill of Creation and all solid ground took form underneath him.

The act of “Sailing” signifies the motion in creation. Motion implies that events occur in the realm of time and space relative to each other, thus, the phenomenal universe comes into existence as a mass of moving essence we call the elements. Prior to this motion, there was the primeval state of being without any form and without existence in time or space. The gods and goddesses of the boat form the court of Kheper-Ra.

As Ra, the Supreme Being governed the earth for many thousands of years. He created the world, the planets, the stars and the galaxies; he also created animals, as well as men and women. In the beginning, men and women revered the Divine, but after living for a very long time, they began to take Ra for granted. They became arrogant and vain. Ra sent his daughter, Hetheru, to punish them, but she forgot her way and became lost in the world. Then He left for his abode in heaven and gave the earthly throne to his son Shu, and daughter, Tefnut. After a long period of time, they turned over the throne to their children, Geb and Nut. After some time again, Geb and Nut gave the throne to their children, Asar and Aset, and so on in a line of succession throughout history, down to the Pharaohs of Kamit.

So, the Shetaut Neter “Mystery teachings” were originally given by the Creator, Khepri.
