highlights.text: Here, Nārada is saying that those who have faith, devotion and have cultivated that bhakti, attain God-realisation.
no? And when you are in the company of the devotees, you can feel the presence of God.
This is a characteristic of a devotee. Through devotion he transcends worldly desire and bondage. He doesn’t retain any interest in a worldly matter.

‘Na kiñcid vāñchati’: The devotees rise above all earthly needs and wants. Their hearts are filled with peace and perfect satisfaction. They don’t have any desire for anything. They are conscious about what is real and what is not real. They have that awareness of discrimination.

Here Nārada is saying that the devotees who have attained the bliss of love are freed from grief. Just like darkness: when a light is brought, darkness disappears. Grief, which is a mental state, is created by the mind. Why does one grieve?

But when the mind starts that inner journey and dives within that ocean of bliss and gets absorbed in the love within the heart, there is no place for grieving. Pain and grief can’t approach such a devotee.

You can see in the world when people hate each other. Are they free? They can never be free. Are they at peace? They can never be at peace. Because they have taken the aspect of hate into their hearts, every action, whatever they do, will be filled with that hate. Even if they appear to be peaceful on the outside, they will never be at peace with themselves. So, ‘na dveṣṭi’ says those devotees who have realised and have had darśan, seen God and perceived Him, are free and don’t have hate in their hearts.
A devotee hates no one. He loves all and helps everybody. Whatever the devotee does is for the upbringing of humanity.
Devotees who have felt and experienced that divine ecstasy of Love don’t feel any worldly object will ever give them personal happiness. Devotees may not like something, but they don’t hate anything.
One perceives that everything is just a manifestation of the Supreme Lord Himself. All that is moving and unmoving, everything, is just His play, His divine līlā.

This is the nature of Bhagavān: when there is love, He likes to steal. This is His personal relationship with His devotee. When your vision has changed and is not impaired by limitation, then His divine play starts in your life. And who will really recognise that divine play? It’s only those who are in tune with Him. Only those who you can call yours will come and play with you, not somebody who is not yours.
That doesn’t mean that you can’t have children. It doesn’t mean that you can’t have a big house. You can have them. But the urge, that longing, that dependency is not there.
A true devotee works at every moment realising that, ‘I am serving my beloved Lord in whatever. And whatever I am having is for His sake, in His service.’

So very often we have expectations that God will come the way we want Him to come. Sometimes He will come in the form of a dog. He has endless forms. There is no end. His power is infinite. His forms are infinite. Arjuna, when he perceived Bhagavān everywhere, saw that there was not a single place where He was not present.

‘Notsāhī bhavati’: To attain that mahā-bhāva, one has to be disciplined with oneself, one has to be disciplined by constant awareness. He said that everything on the outside can be taken away. You are enthusiastic and ecstatic about things which can be taken. You are ecstatic about things which are perishable. You are ecstatic about things that have a beginning and have an end. But the devotees are absorbed in divine bliss which no one can steal.

When your heart is fully filled with that bliss, when your heart is filled with that love, there is no desire, because the ego is not there. There is no separation. Because everything has been consumed by Him.
In devotion, you transcend this duality of good and bad, you transcend all the limitations which the mind has created. How could you become a divine instrument if you are so focused upon yourself?
Only when you start reflecting the love of God do you become a divine being. And that’s what sūtra number five says about it.

In this verse, Nārada is describing a person who has attained that peak of devotion, one who has drowned himself in that ocean of bliss. Nārada gives a clear understanding of bhakti. Those who have attained that state of bhakti, those who have been completely submerged in that ocean of love and devotion, abandon everything and have complete surrender to the Feet of God.

Here, Bhagavān is talking about an eternal intoxication of God’s Love where He takes complete charge of everything. For those who are the vessels of the Divine, they are completely in tune with whatever tune He wants to play. They move as God desires for them to move.
But now you have to get to know it. You have to get to know that Supreme Being, not just play and dance in His tune, but get to know Him. And how will you get to know Him?

Those devotees who remain in that divine ecstasy of the Lord, those whose minds are fully merged into the svarūpa of Bhagavān are absent from this world. They are not aware of what is happening around them. They laugh, they weep, they cry, they sing, they scream, they dance in that divine ecstasy.
The ecstasy which Nārada is talking about, the ecstasy of love, is a God-intoxicated devotee: those who are not conscious of themselves, and those who are eternally into this deep absorption.
‘Stabdho bhavati’: Whatever their action is, it is not with their minds that they are acting, but it is the Supreme Lord Himself who is governing every act of them.

Uddhava loved Kṛṣṇa so much that he looked like Kṛṣṇa. When he went to the gopīs, they did not recognise him; they thought that he was Kṛṣṇa. (It was only when he started talking that they said, ‘No, no, no, no, no, you are not our Kṛṣṇa.’ Then they wanted to beat him!) Such it is when one is completely surrendered. His perfection, that infinite bliss, that joy, reflects through your being completely.

But it is a state where one’s mind is not attached to anything. A monk can appear very nice and holy, but his mind is still fully attached to the world. And others can appear to be in the world, but their minds are fully absorbed in the Divine.

But now, that doesn’t mean anything for you. Now there is a different aim in your life, isn’t there? That’s why it is said that bhakti is not led by desire; it is fixed. One has found a different kind of expression, and one has found that everything that they knew before is of no use now.

Nārada said, no, those whose hearts are burning with bhakti, they don’t even want that acknowledgement of God. They just love Him for the sake of love. They just love Him for the sake of His pleasure, His happiness.
That’s why He said that the basis of bhakti is self-restraint. So, renunciation is the very essence of one’s devotional practice and love.

If you want to control the mind, you can’t do it just like that. Start to control it step by step. But to control it, you have to have that willingness to transform. If you don’t have that willingness to transform, you will never change.
Here He said, ‘No, My devotee.’ Here Bhagavān again said, ‘My devotee, you belong to Me. All that you do.’
‘What I am concerned about is that intention. I am not concerned about your actions only on the outside, but your intention on how you are doing this action is very important.’

Sūtra number eight gives a specific definition of renunciation. Those bhaktas who have attained the state of divine union have no interest in the pleasure of this world nor do they have any desire left for this world to come.

Here Nārada said learn to discriminate, learn to reduce the activities. How would you do that? By fully absorbing into bhajan, sādhana, and doing Nāma-japam. The more your mind is absorbed into the Divine Name, the more you will be away from fulfilling all these unwanted desires.

‘Loka-veda-vyāpāra’: What am I renouncing? I am renouncing all worldly activities. I am renouncing all the Vedic rituals, the scriptural duty. These activities that are written in the scriptures are only for those who are still on the path. They need a certain direction. Scriptural duty is the transformation, when there is no pride, there is no ego, there is no selfishness, there is no attachment, there is no craving, there is no, ‘Yes, I want something. I am doing a certain ritual because I want to gain something’.

But for those whose minds are fully absorbed in the Lord, everything that they do is an offering to the Supreme Lord. Every thought they have is only for Him. All work is an expression of His love. Whatever they do is an expression of His love. They are in divine union with Him. They are in deep absorption with Him. They have fully surrendered to Him. They are doing only His will.
They only chant the ritual, they only chant the mantra, and then that’s it, finish. But they are not absorbed. Their heart doesn’t call for the Lord. Their heart doesn’t feel anything.
They perform all the activities like all normal beings, but their minds are not attached to the action on the outside, their minds are attached only to the Supreme and they offer everything unto Him.

When we are talking about kriyā-yoga, what does that stand for? It stands for the absorption in ‘in whatever action I am doing, God is with me and I am doing it for Him’. That is kriyā-yoga. ‘Every one of my actions is for His pleasure. Every action is a reminder of Him.’
‘Yes, I am working, I don’t have time to chant.’ You have time to look at your phone, you have time to look at your Facebook, you have time to look at your email.

Mīrābāī said, ‘I have given up my mind, my heart, my soul, my intellect, I have given my whole being to my beloved Giridhār Gopāla.’ In that state of self-surrender, the Supreme Lord Himself becomes dear to such a devotee. That bhakta has made the Supreme Lord a servant. He is bound. It’s not the Lord who is binding the devotee. It is that deep absorption of grace which descends upon the devotee which makes Bhagavān Himself a slave to the bhakta. And this is that absolute self-surrender.

Understand that. ‘Only when you completely surrender to Me, can I take complete charge of you. If you do not surrender completely to Me, I can’t take charge of you. Until then you are fully in the clutches of the world of māyā.’

When the child is thinking about the mother, no one tells the child that they have to think about the mother. It is natural that the child is thinking about the mother. have spent a significant portion of my life being afraid to see myself fully because it came with the potential risk of punishment, abandonment, rejection. Fortunately, unlike your ancestors, you’re (probably) not facing death every day. In fact, in many parts of the world, life has never been safer. Yet, your survival mechanism hasn’t changed much. Your brain still scans your environment looking for potential threats.

In many ways, some parts of your brain have become obsolete. While you may not be seconds away from being eaten by a predator, your brain still gives significantly more weight to adverse events than to positive ones.
Therefore, you learned to look for any sign of rejection, and this became hardwired in your brain. Nowadays, being rejected often carries little or no consequence to your long-term survival.

While you are fortunate to have such a useful survival mechanism, it is also your responsibility to separate real threats from imaginary ones. If you don’t, you’ll experience unnecessary pain and worry that will negatively impact the quality of your life.
One of a human being’s greatest powers is our ability to use our thoughts to shape our reality and interpret events in a more empowering way. This book will teach you how to do this.

In the past, dopamine directly linked to our survival, now, it can be stimulated artificially. A great example of this effect is social media, which uses psychology to suck as much time as possible out of your life. Have you noticed all these notifications that pop up regularly? They’re used to trigger a release of dopamine so you stay connected, and the longer you stay connected, the more money the services make.

Today’s society is selling a version of happiness that can make us unhappy. We’ve become addicted to dopamine mainly because of marketers who have found effective ways to exploit our brains. We receive multiple shots of dopamine throughout the day and we love it. But is that the same thing as happiness?

Your mind quickly acclimates to new situations, which is probably the result of evolution and our need to adapt continually to survive and reproduce. This acclimatization is also probably why the new car or house you want will only make you happy for a while. Once the initial excitement wears off, you’ll move on to crave the next exciting thing. This phenomenon is known as ‘hedonic adaptation.’
What it means is that, in the long run, external events have minimal impact on your level of happiness.

In fact, according to Sonja Lyubomirsky, author of The How of Happiness, fifty percent of our happiness is determined by genetics, forty percent by internal factors, and only ten percent by external factors. These external factors include such things as whether we’re single or married, rich or poor, and similar social influences.
The influence of external factors is probably way less than you thought. The bottom line is this: Your attitude towards life influences your happiness, not what happens to you.

The ego refers to the self-identity you’ve constructed throughout your life. How was this identity created? Put simply, the ego was created through your thoughts and, as a mind-created identity, has no concrete reality.
Events that happen to you bear no meaning in themselves. You give them meaning only through your interpretation of those events.
Note that the ego is neither good nor bad; it’s just a result of a lack of self-awareness. It fades away as you become aware of it since ego and awareness cannot coexist.

Your ego is a selfish entity, only concerned about its survival. Interestingly, it’s somewhat similar to your brain in the way it operates. It has its survival mechanism and will do whatever it can to persist. As with your brain, its primary concern is neither your happiness nor your peace of mind. On the contrary, your ego is restless. It wants you to be a go-getter. It wants you to do, acquire and achieve great things so you can become a ‘somebody.’
Most people derive their self-worth from their physical appearance. Your ego loves the way you look because it is the easiest thing to recognize and quantify.

The ego also derives its sense of identity from your relationships with others. The ego is only interested in what it can get from them. In other words, the ego thrives on the way it can use people to strengthen its identity.

Some parents’ egos lead to the creation of a strong sense of attachment and identification with their children. This attachment is based on the false belief their children are their ‘possessions.’ As a result, they try to control their childrens’ lives and ‘use’ them to live the life they wanted to live when they were younger—this is called living vicariously through your children.

The feeling of needing someone is very much a play of the ego as well. Anthony de Mello has a beautiful way to put it when he says: Loneliness is not cured by human company. Loneliness is cured by contact with reality, by understanding that we don’t need people.
Once you realize you don’t actually need anyone, you can start enjoying people’s company. You can see them as they really are rather than trying to get something from them.

Your ego also uses beliefs to strengthen its identity. In extreme cases, people become so attached to their beliefs they are ready to die to protect them. Worse still, they are willing to kill people who disagree with them. Religion is a perfect illustration of the dangers of excessive attachment to beliefs. The ego will use any belief to strengthen its identity, whether these beliefs are religious, political, or metaphysical.

Here are some main aspects of the ego: The ego tends to equate ‘having’ with ‘being,’ which is why the ego likes to identify with objects. The ego lives through comparison. Your ego likes to compare itself with other egos. The ego is never satisfied. Your ego always wants more. More fame, more stuff, more recognition, and so on. The ego’s sense of self-worth often depends on the worth you have in the eyes of others. Your ego needs the approval of other people to feel valued.

In short, most of your emotions are based on your personal story and the way you perceive the world. As you replace your current story with a more empowering one—while, at the same time, letting go of your excessive attachment to things, people or ideas—you will be able to experience more positive emotions. Later in this book, we’ll see how you can change the way you interpret events.

The first thing to understand is that emotions come and go. One moment you feel happy, the next you feel sad. While you do have some control over your emotions, you must also recognize their unpredictable nature.

To start taking control of your emotions you must accept they are transient. You must learn to let them pass without feeling the need to identify strongly with them. You must allow yourself to feel sad without adding commentaries such as, “I shouldn’t be sad,” or “What’s wrong with me?” Instead, you must allow reality to just be.
Remember this: the way you interpret emotions, as well as the blame game you engage in, creates suffering, not the emotions themselves.

Negative emotions often serve a purpose. They may serve as a wake-up call. They may help you learn something positive about yourself. Of course, when you’re under their spell, it may be difficult to look at the bright side of things, but in hindsight, you may realize emotions—even sad ones—had their role to play in your ultimate success.

Emotions work the same way. They signal you to do something about your current situation. Perhaps, you need to let go of some people, quit your job, or remove a disempowering story that creates suffering in your life.
No matter how depressed you are, how much grief you’re experiencing, or how horrible you feel at a given point in time, this shall pass.
Your emotions come and they go. Your depression will go, your sadness will vanish and your anger will fade away.

Have you ever felt you’ll never be happy again? Have you ever been so attached to your emotions you thought they’ll never go away? Don’t worry; it’s a common feeling. Negative emotions act as a filter that taints the quality of your experiences. During a negative episode, every experience is perceived through this filter. While the world outside may remain the same, you will experience it in a completely different way based on how you feel.

You may now believe that, armed with the knowledge you have gained from this book, you’ll never be depressed again. Wrong! You’ll keep experiencing sadness, frustration, depression, or resentment, but hopefully, each time these occur, you’ll become wiser and wiser, remembering that this too, shall pass

Interestingly, external factors might not be—and often aren’t—the direct cause of a sudden change in your emotional state. You can be in the same situation, with the same job, the same amount of money in your bank account, and have the same problems as always, but experience radically different emotional states.

I encourage you to make a conscious effort to notice whenever such events happen and start seeing through your emotions’ trickery. You might want to go one step further and record these events in a journal.

An emotion usually represents an amplified energized thought pattern, and because of its often-overpowering energetic charges, it is not easy initially to stay present enough to be able to watch it. It wants to take you over, and it usually succeeds—unless there is enough presence in you.

Negative emotions are like a spell. While you’re under their influence, breaking free from them seems impossible. You may know dwelling on the same thoughts is pointless, yet you can’t help but go along with the flow. Feeling an intense pull, you keep identifying with your thoughts and, as a result, feel worse and worse. When this happens, no rational argument seems to work.

Often, a vicious circle builds up between your thinking and the emotion: they feed each other. The thought pattern creates a magnified reflection of itself in the form of an emotion, and the vibrational frequency of the emotion keeps feeding the original thought pattern.
One day, as I was observing my thought process, I realized experiencing pain in my knees negatively affected my mood, triggering more negative emotions in a negative feedback loop.

Thus, to reduce negative emotions, you must learn to compartmentalize your issues. Don’t let your mind over-dramatize things by clustering unrelated matters. It will only make you feel worse. Instead, remember that negative emotions exist only in your mind. Taken separately, most of your issues aren’t such a big deal, and no rule that says you have to solve them all at once.

We previously saw you attract thoughts that matched your emotional state. The opposite is also true. You can’t attract thoughts that are out of sync with how you feel at any given time. Even if you tried to think positive thoughts, your mind wouldn’t be receptive to them.
Whenever you feel pain, your first reaction is to interpret it. When you do so, you generate negative thoughts. Your identification with these thoughts is what creates mental suffering.

title: Mentchu-Hotep and the Spirit of the Medjay
author: Mfundishi Jhutyms Salim

highlights.text: We are light energy beings; thus, the Kemety cosmogram, ontology, and epistemology center the power of the sun and calls it Ra. It centers the power of Amen, black kem of Kemet, as a force likewise capable of producing light.

It is a hierarchal system of highly disciplined men who, in secret societies, developed their manhood in years for mastery under a special Jegna (mental, physical, and spiritual guides that help you on your special mission in life).
Their spiritual gifts were natural in Ntchr and followed an age-old regiment in the sciences.
It was likely three hundred or more, alluding to an older secret widespread order that was in existence in Kemet, the chosen predecessors on a divine mission.
Like our great and victorious spiritual warriors of our glorious Afrakan past, we must reclaim and resurrect the Heru consciousness lying dormant in our black Afrakan minds.

“Mentchu-hotep, my son, listen carefully to what I’m about to say to you. Every soul, every culture, every land has something profound to teach us about what our journey to earth is all about and what the spirit world is trying to say to us. You must learn to make wise choices as a leader. We need to always bear in mind the resources that are ours to use.
Wealth’s primary function was to enable one to be generous and to bring balance where there was none.

Become very watchful, careful, and aware of your thoughts, beliefs, and motives. “Just remember this, my son Mentchu-hotep, even if you don’t know the answer, spirit knows, even if you don’t know the reason, spirit knows. In all matters and in all things, allow your life to be guided by the Divine Spirit.

“The proper and greatest way to learn is to acquire learning directly from nature. When the Divine Spirit is guiding you, no formal studies are necessary. You will be fine, son. The mystery of life isn’t a problem to solve but a reality to experience.” She looked at her growing son with so much pride. “Open your heart to the beauty in life, and your life will reflect that beauty in your heart. Remember, my son, a peaceful heart within makes beauty without.”
Remember, you are not a person, you just experience that you are. You are a divine spirit.”
A person’s worldly experience is an optical delusion of their consciousness created by the ego. We must always focus on the one, never the symbols but only the symptoms.”
To the ancient mind of the Medjay, animals, plants, and humans were parts of one large earthly family.
These Ntchru are laws and principles of creation and act as the managers of all existence for all life known and unknown.
The Khemmennu Ntchru were eight deities who were the basis of the Kemet’s creation myth during the second golden age.

“The nature of self is to understand the nature of the Ntchru. The eyes with which we see the Ntchru are the same eyes with which the Ntchru see us. Therefore, it is important for us to learn to see with our hearts and our minds for it is only with the heart, an aspect of our minds, that one can see righteously.
Remember, the Divine Spirit is not in the world. How can it be in a world that isn’t there? The Divine Spirit is in your mind. That’s where both the problem and the answer are.”

All the great Nswt Bety’s, masters, priests, and divine teachers of the past and present have placed great emphasis upon the quality of our thoughts. They have demonstrated throughout their teachings how thought can and does modify our environment and experiences.

“The higher self, the divine mind within each of us, I must learn how to let it guide my thoughts, my reasoning, and my actions. We are destined, Neferu, to become creators of peace and harmony. We must strengthen our ability to love compassionately and unconditionally. I promise to return to you with a greater spirit and a greater love.”

“Never allow the fears of others to become your fears. Never allow the limitations of others to become your limitations. Ride a higher wave. The wave of the Medjay is the way of Divine Spirit. Know that other possibilities exist for your life, Mentchu-hotep. I say this not as just the Hem Sem Tepy of this sacred temple, but as a fellow Medjay.”

“A true spiritual teacher helps to awaken your power by leading you back to your greatest you. By reminding you that you are a unique expression of Ntchr and have every right to be who you are and what your soul aspires to be. Such a teacher will never demand that you stand in awe of his/her light.
“When training with outsiders, never let your opponent know all that you know. You might have to meet that same opponent on the battlefield.”

We created weapons that were extensions of our own bodies, minds, and souls. Each Medjay’s weapon was part of his or her consciousness following the symmetry of our own molecular structure, using the golden ratio or golden spiral.

He was saying an initiate is one who has penetrated into the understanding and innerstanding of the vital matrix not just knowledge that results from the sensory observation of appearances, which the mind has created, but also we are learning the science of Divine Spirit.

This is the opposite of what the world thinks, and even most of the people I know think who are not Medjay or spiritual priests. If nothing is outside of your mind, then to judge it is to grant it power over you and to not judge it is to withdraw its power over you. I will have to work on that skill.

class. As I meditated on some of the Medjay training methods of combat, I realized that they were founded on the inner esoteric system of perceiving not only the world, but also the cosmos just like the Mdw Ntchr.

“You must forget about the boat, forget about Hapy, and imagine they don’t exist, which they don’t. Remember, you are the captain of your own ship, and your existence shares the same harmonious reality of Ma’at. You are urged to develop a relationship with the Divine Spirit.

“Before I talk about this common illusion that we share as a nation, I want you, mighty Medjay warriors, to know you are mighty spirits connected to the one Divine Spirit. You are far greater than you think. What you see me do, you are capable of doing and even far greater things. People are spirits. They just don’t know it. And how can you really be a person if you’re not a body? And you are not your body. In Barwat, I will explain the mind and the ego, but now it is nation time.”

The selection of our Shemsu Heru requires the consent of nobles and priests, and an unpopular ruler could be removed. Ma’at was developed here, and no one is exempted from Ma’at—not even the Shemsu Heru or his royal family.
I beginning to understand what he was trying to convey to me: that even in the eye of a mighty storm, there is peace, and you must find that peace under or in any condition.

The chief Medjay said you must learn how to choose between the Divine Spirit who represents the real you and the part of your mind that represents the false you created by the ego.

The reason I keep a photo of that house is that it changed my life. To find that house and to move into it was my first act, as an adult, that embraced the idea of ambition.
Ambition, I have come to believe, is the most primal and sacred fundament of our being. To feel ambition and to act upon it is to embrace the unique calling of our souls. Not to act upon that ambition is to turn our backs on ourselves and on the reason for our existence

In the shadow life, we live in denial and we act by addiction. We pursue callings that take us nowhere and permit ourselves to be controlled by compulsions that we cannot understand (or are not aware of ) and whose outcomes serve only to keep us caged, unconscious and going nowhere.

I had friends who were living out shadow movies, or creating shadow art, or initiating shadow industries. These were our addictions, and we worked them for all they were worth. There was only one problem: none of us was writing a real novel, or painting a real painting, or starting a real business. We were amateurs living in the past or dreaming of the future, while failing utterly to do the work necessary to progress in the present.
When craft, dedication, and professionalism come together, the result can be astonishing. Sometimes the work even achieves immortality.
The amateur is an egotist. He takes the material of his personal pain and uses it to draw attention to himself. He creates a “life,” a “character,” a “personality.”

The pre-addictive individual—i.e., you and I when we’re young—experiences a calling. To art, to service, to honorable sacrifice. In other words, we experience positive aspiration. A vision of the higher, realized self we might become.

What makes this moment so soul-precarious is that most of us are unconscious, in the event, of both our aspirations and our Resistance. We’re asleep. We know only that something is wrong and we don’t know how to fix it. We’re restless. We’re bored. We’re angry. We burn to accomplish something great, but we don’t know where to begin and, even if we did, we’d be so terrified that we still couldn’t take a step

Instead, the addict enacts his aspiration in shadow form. The addiction becomes his novel, his adventure, his great love. The work of art or service that might have been produced is replaced by the drama, conflict, and suffering of the addict’s crazy, haunted, shattered life.

Robert McKee, in his story seminars, testifies that the essential quality in a fictional protagonist—i.e., the hero in a book or a movie—is that he or she must possess the passion and the will to push the story to the limits of human experience in order to achieve their goal.

Addictions are not “bad.” They are simply the shadow forms of a more noble and exalted calling. Our addictions are our callings themselves, only encrypted and incognito.
They are a metaphor for our best selves, the coded version of our higher aspirations

You and I, who are artists and entrepreneurs, live a life that’s closer to natural, if you ask me.
We migrate, too. We follow the Muse instead of the sun. When one crop is picked, we hit the road and move on to the next

All addictions share, among others, two primary qualities.
1. They embody repetition without progress.
2. They produce incapacity as a payoff.

Distraction and displacement seem innocent on the surface. How can we be harming ourselves by having fun, or seeking romance, or enjoying the fruits of this big, beautiful world?
But lives go down the tubes one repetition at a time, one deflection at a time, one hundred and forty characters at a time.
The following is a sampling, in no particular order, of garden-variety addictions that fall short of hard-core chemical dependency but are still more than potent enough to cripple, malform, and destroy our lives

My own theory is that the obsessive pursuit of sex is an attempt to obliterate the ego, i.e., “normal” consciousness, the monkey-mind that tortures us with restlessness, fear, anger, and self-centeredness.
We’re trying to get to the level above that.
The entity we’re seeking union with is ourselves.
We’re trying to connect with our true being, our soul, our Self.

Resistance hates two qualities above all others: concentration and depth. Why? Because when we work with focus and we work deep, we succeed.
How did Tom Brady master the art of the forward pass? How did Picasso paint? How did Yo-Yo Ma learn the cello?
Resistance wants to keep us shallow and unfocused. So it makes the superficial and the vain intoxicating

But when we’re addicted to money, we become hooked on the metaphor.
Is money how we keep score? Is it magic? Is wealth a currency that opens doors, realizes possibilities, produces transcendence?
Money is second only to sex in the richness of its metaphor. But, as in the case of carnality, our real object is the currency of our own hearts. (The same premise applies to power, fame, and all other external expressions of potency.)

The payoff for the prisoner is release from the agonizing imperative of identifying, embracing and bringing into material existence the dreams and visions of his own deepest, noblest, and most honorable heart

The artist and the addict both wrestle with this experience of exile. They share an acute, even excruciating sensitivity to the state of separation and isolation, and both actively seek a way to overcome it, to transcend it, or at least to make the pain go away
It’s the condition of being suspended between two worlds and being unable to fully enter into either

You and I are called to the upper realm (and it is calling to us), but we’re having a pretty good time (sometimes) down here in the sphere of the senses. Bottom line: we’re marooned in the middle, stuck inside of Mobile with the Memphis blues again
It’s not just the Irish. The pain of being human is that we’re all angels imprisoned in vessels of flesh.

The habits and addictions of the amateur are conscious or unconscious self-inflicted wounds. Their payoff is incapacity. When we take our M1903 Springfield and blow a hole in our foot, we no longer have to face the real fight of our lives, which is to become who we are and to realize our destiny and our calling

Fear is the primary color of the amateur’s interior world. Fear of failure, fear of success, fear of looking foolish, fear of under-achieving and fear of over-achieving, fear of poverty, fear of loneliness, fear of death

The amateur dreads becoming who she really is because she fears that this new person will be judged by others as “different.” The tribe will declare us “weird” or “queer” or “crazy.” The tribe will reject us.
Here’s the truth: the tribe doesn’t give a shit.
There is no tribe.
That gang or posse that we imagine is sustaining us by the bonds we share is in fact a conglomeration of individuals who are just as fucked up as we are and just as terrified. Each individual is so caught up in his own bullshit that he doesn’t have two seconds to worry about yours or mine, or to reject or diminish us because of it.

When we truly understand that the tribe doesn’t give a damn, we’re free. There is no tribe, and there never was.
Our lives are entirely up to us

When we turn pro, everything becomes simple. Our aim centers on the ordering of our days in such a way that we overcome the fears that have paralyzed us in the past.
We now structure our hours not to flee from fear, but to confront it and overcome it. We plan our activities in order to accomplish an aim. And we bring our will to bear so that we stick to this resolution

When we turn pro, we will be compelled to make painful choices. There will be people who in the past had been colleagues and associates, even friends, whom we will no longer be able to spend time with if our intention is to grow and to evolve. We will have to choose between the life we want for our future and the life we have left behind

The professional displays courage, not only in the roles she embraces (which invariably scare the hell out of her) or the sacrifices she makes (of time, love, family) or even in the enduring of criticism, blame, envy, and lack of understanding, but above all in the confronting of her own doubts and demons

When we do the work for itself alone (I know how easy that is to say and how hard it is to do), we’re like that Marine who sleeps in a foxhole in the freezing rain but who knows a secret that only he and his brothers and sisters share.
When we do the work for itself alone, our pursuit of a career (or a living or fame or wealth or notoriety) turns into something else, something loftier and nobler, which we may never even have thought about or aspired to at the beginning.
It turns into a practice

To “have a practice” in yoga, say, or tai chi, or calligraphy, is to follow a rigorous, prescribed regimen with the intention of elevating the mind and the spirit to a higher level.
A practice implies engagement in a ritual. A practice may be defined as the dedicated, daily exercise of commitment, will, and focused intention aimed, on one level, at the achievement of mastery in a field but, on a loftier level, intended to produce a communion with a power greater than ourselves—call it whatever you like: God, mind, soul, Self, the Muse, the superconscious
Our intention as artists is to get better, to go deeper, to work closer and closer to the bone

Each day we, as professionals, face the same monsters and chimeras as did Perseus or Bellerophon or St. George.
The sword master advancing into ritual combat has inwardly made peace with his own extinction. He is prepared to leave everything, including his life, there on the fighting floor.

Your influences are already shaping your work. Every writer absorbs from what they read.
This book gives you the strategy. By the final page, you will have a method for transforming any writer you admire into fuel for your own original work.

García Márquez colonized my voice for two years. His rhythms entered my prose and refused to leave. Every paragraph carried his cadence before it carried mine. The gap between what the writing attempted and what it achieved announced itself on every page. Reproducing the surface took effort. Reaching the engine proved impossible.

In 1800, William Wordsworth published his Preface to Lyrical Ballads and defined poetry as "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings." The sentence turned into a manifesto. Poetry, and by extension all creative work, emerged from emotion, from the soul. The creator received; the creator did not build.

The Romantics, reacting against Enlightenment rationalism and industrial standardization, celebrated the individual creative genius as a figure apart from society, touched by divine inspiration, creating from pure imagination.

That advice followed me everywhere when writing first took hold. Find your voice. Write the story only you can tell. It sounded brilliant on the page. In practice it read like trying to follow a recipe that listed "inspiration" as the first ingredient and provided no measurements for anything else.
The imagination rearranges; it does not create from a vacuum.

Where originality means creating from nothing, aspiring writers face an impossible task. Originality has never meant that. Originality means making combinations nobody has made before, arranging existing elements in configurations that surprise and produce effects no prior arrangement has produced. The raw materials stay borrowed. The combination is where the originality lives.

García Márquez did the most damage. His voice colonized mine with such depth that no paragraph could be written without hearing his rhythms. The lyrical density, the mythic register, the sentences that bent time: all of it absorbed.

"Write the story only you can tell" offers no instruction for the writer whose stories still sound like other people's. It diagnoses the symptom (your voice is borrowed) and prescribes a cure (find your real voice) without specifying the treatment. The advice assumes a destination and provides no route.

Bloom argued that every strong poet struggles against the influence of precursor poets, engaging in a kind of Oedipal combat to clear imaginative space for their own work. The "anxiety" in his title refers to the psychological burden of coming after greatness: the dread of being derivative, the struggle to produce more than an echo.

Every writer exists in conversation with the dead. The writers who came before created the language, the forms, the possibilities within which you work. When you write a sentence, you operate with tools they sharpened. When you structure a story, you use architectures they built.

The Introduction traced Cormac McCarthy's journey from Faulkner copyist to the author of Blood Meridian, a novel Harold Bloom called "the greatest single book since Faulkner's As I Lay Dying." That transformation took two decades. The pattern it illustrates is universal: influence absorbed in full turns invisible, and the combination of multiple digested influences produces something new.

When you write, you hear every echo. You know which sentence structure came from Didion, which rhythm came from copying Denis Johnson stories late at night. The borrowed elements announce themselves in your head. They feel like confessions.

Your readers encounter your prose without access to your reading history. What feels like obvious theft registers to them, if it registers at all, as style. The echoes you hear at full volume reach them as whispers, mixed into a voice that functions as unified even when you know it is composite.
Where creativity is combinatorial, your job as a writer is to combine better. Choose your influences with intention. Study them with purpose. Extract what serves your needs and discard what does not.
The cure for sounding too much like one writer is absorbing five more until they all interfere with each other and what emerges sounds like you.

The shift happened in an unexpected register: blog articles, written in English, aimed at an audience that could be pictured rather than a literary tradition that could not be reached. The conversational tone forced an exit from every imitation practiced up to that point. Márquez does not write blog posts. Hemingway does not write blog posts. The form demanded something the borrowed voices could not provide, and what filled the gap turned out to be mine.

My early twenties brought ambition that outpaced ability by a ratio measurable on the page. Fitzgerald drew me toward lyrical elegance, sentences that glided. Palahniuk drew me toward transgressive energy, sentences that hit. Both qualities lived in writers I admired. Both sat available to anyone willing to study and practice. When the attempt came, the prose collapsed.

The failure, at the time, looked personal, as if some writers could combine influences and others could not. The actual problem ran simpler and more fixable: neither influence had been absorbed to sufficient depth for the fusion to turn organic. The ingredients went into the pot before the cooking had been learned.
How that arrangement works, what makes some combinations succeed and others produce wreckage, is the difference between building a voice and hoping one arrives.
The word "original" comes from the Latin originalis, meaning "belonging to the origin" or "of the source." An original work has origins, sources, traceable beginnings. It comes from somewhere.

Prose works the same way. Your vocabulary arrived from the language you were born into. Your sentence structures run on patterns that existed before you. Your techniques for creating tension, building character, managing time: inherited from writers you read, with awareness or without. The specific combinations you make, filtered through your obsessions and limitations: your contribution lives there.

Young had spent decades at J. Walter Thompson, one of the largest advertising agencies in the world. His central claim demolished Shelley's myth from the inside: an idea is nothing more nor less than a new combination of old elements. The capacity to bring old elements into new combinations depends on the ability to see relationships. This ability can be cultivated.
The writer combines words, sentence patterns, narrative strategies, thematic concerns. Nobody works from nothing. Everyone works from combination.

In 1990, the British cognitive scientist Margaret Boden published The Creative Mind: Myths and Mechanisms and identified three forms of creativity, the first and most relevant being combinational creativity, producing unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas. Boden grounded the Romantic mystery in cognitive mechanics. What the brain does, at every level, is store and recombine.

That last point carries the weight. Eliot could assemble fragments because his technical command allowed seamless transitions between registers. McCarthy could fuse Faulkner's syntax with Melville's register because his ear for rhythm made the fusion coherent. Thompson could channel Fitzgerald's precision and Hemingway's force into something manic and new because his typing apprenticeship had given him physical command of those rhythms.
You can see the influences because they haven't been transformed.
The voice in those stories, lyrical and damaged and starving for God, sounded unprecedented. Readers couldn't place it.

What makes the combination Johnson's own: his obsessions. Johnson struggled with addiction for years. By his own account, he entered his first psychiatric ward for alcohol at twenty-one. The terrain of Jesus' Son maps that struggle: emergency rooms, flophouses, highways, moments of chemical ecstasy and physical wreckage. His influences gave him tools. His life gave him subject matter. The fusion of inherited technique with personal urgency produced something none of his influences had written.

Mind Magic is a system of magick that teaches you to use your mind-body connection, your intention, and the power of your observation to alter the configuration of your current reality into one that is more desirable.
In a nutshell, Mind Magic is the practice of using a set of structured methodologies to work powerful magick with only your mind.
Mind Magic does away with the need for external entities, objects, and circumstances to help you work an enchantment. Instead, we will dive within You to activate real magick for positive change.
You have the ability within yourself to work powerful magick all on your own
Learn to use these methods systematically and yet consciously, saturating the power of your observation with your focused intent, and you will be working magick.

This book gives you the building blocks and the structure to create your own magick. The methods you will learn here are flexible enough that you can customize them a bit to your own preferences. They are tools for your magickal toolbox. You will learn to pull them out and use them at will.

Mind Magic is simply a method of engaging your whole mind to influence that already changing, fluxing world around you to take the path of change that you choose for it—to put unseen energies in motion to alter your reality.

Within the pages of this text, you may find some golden nuggets—ideas which, once planted inside your mind, have the power to change forever how you view your every desire, your every aspiration, and every goal you may have for your life.

It’s a way to create your own enchantments using a given set of methodologies so that you can customize your magick to whatever you desire, allowing you to alter virtually any reality in a fun and systematic manner.

To elevate the consciousness of the world, one soul at a time. To help my fellow humans on this earth to find true happiness and deep inner peace. The attempt to “hold onto” faith—that something will happen, that something or someone will get better, that some miracle might occur—all of these have the seed of doubt planted within them.
They aren’t exercising that kind of doubtless faith—that knowingness—that yields great power.
Instead of having faith, I teach you to feel out what you are creating, and then know it is so.

If you were completely aware of what’s going on deep within your mind in all of these situations, the difference between faith and knowing would be quite obvious. We live in a Universe made up of matter and energy that continually interact in an infinitely complex manner. Everything you see, know, or experience is composed of matter and energy. Even your thoughts, emotions, and feelings are a kind of energy.

The ideas of classical mechanics are sensible and logical: Matter is substance. It takes up space. It exists in a given space at a given time. It cannot exist in multiple places at once. Two particles of matter cannot occupy the same space at the same time. And so on.

Matter is energy, not solid substance. It doesn’t really take up space but can exist in a range of space at any given time. It can exist in multiple places at once. And, two particles of matter can occupy the same space at the same time.
Scientists found that what triggered a particle to change from a wave of probabilities to appear as a solid particle at a certain location in space was the observation of it
It is what modern physics calls the “quantum observer effect.” This basically says that the observation of any given experiment will alter the outcome of that experiment.
Regardless of their arguments, it is their observance that causes these “probability waves” of vibrating energy to collapse into seemingly solid particles.
Your own awareness of yourself is enough to validate the existence of your consciousness.
Magick is when the observance of reality changes that reality.

Exercising this power of observation as the cause itself is what differentiates the real magician from everyone else. The magician is still using the natural law of cause and effect, but is creating the desired effect by using magick as the cause.
What we’re going to do with Mind Magic is expand the ability you already have of moving your body with your mind to making other changes to your environment with just your mind.

we have considered that the Universe consists of an infinite complexity of highly-organized energy (including matter). This means that all material substance in the whole Universe is just energy plus the complex structure of that energy.

It is neither an unadorned collection of facts, nor an entirely inward account of what’s going on in your heart and soul. Rather, the journal is the place where the reader takes external information and records it (through the use of quotes, as in the commonplace book); appropriates it through a summary, written in the reader’s own words; and then evaluates it through reflection and personal thought.

Reflect on their meaning for the internal life. The “external things”—be they Platonic philosophy, the actions of an Austen heroine, or a political biography—make us more conscious of our own “reality and shape.” This, not mere accumulation, is the goal of self-education. highlights.text: In Japan, traditional Buddhist monasticism—whether Tendai, Shingon, or Zen—aims at the transcendence of earthly passions. Its basic precepts consist of renouncing all family ties, maintaining celibacy, mastering rigorous disciplines, avoiding contact with the opposite sex, and engaging in elaborate rituals. In contrast, Pure Land is the trans-descendence into the opposite world, the self-awakening to the immersion in the swamp of anger, jealousy, insecurity, fear, addiction, arrogance, hypocrisy.
In the language of Pure Land Buddhism, we who are foolish beings (bonbu) are transformed into the very opposite by the power of great compassion.

Religious awakening does not depend initially on who we are or what we do; rather, it is becoming attuned to the working of great compassion at the heart of existence. This attunement is realized through deep hearing (monpo) of the call from the depth. Nothing is required of us, other than the engagement with deep hearing. Since this is the only requirement—no precepts, no meditative practices, no doctrinal knowledge, it is known as the “easy path.”
the call must become embodied in a person. Embodying means living the nembutsu from which flows the spontaneous saying of namu-amida-butsu.

The wonder of the nembutsu path is that it makes no demands upon a person to become wiser, better, or more perfect. But it does ask us to become authentically real as human beings by awakening to the boundless compassion that sustains us.
“You don’t run away from your troubles and then find happiness. Rather, you no longer think of troubles as troubles. And troubles of themselves turn into happiness, namu-amida-butsu.”

But on the Pure Land path it is those aspects of ourselves that we want to get rid of that are priceless, for they are the primary concern of great compassion that transforms them into cherished, valuable possessions.

The transformation of bits of rubble into gold is due solely to the working of the Primal Vow. Originating in the mythic past, the bodhisattva by the name of Dharmakara identified with the pains of all living beings and attempted to find solutions to human suffering. Expending countless eons of time in suprahuman resolve, reflection, and praxis, Dharmakara fulfilled the Primal Vow to save all beings. This resulted in the attainment of Buddhahood known as Amida, the Buddha of Immeasurable Light and Life. This drama of salvation is contained in the Name, namu-amida-butsu, which resounds throughout the universe.
Now, the Primal Vow works to salvage humankind’s heartbreaks and shattered dreams, transforming them into sources of a rich and full life.

The ten kalpas required to fulfill the Primal Vow suggests the immensity of its profound undertaking—how to uproot the darkness of ignorance inherent in each human being from the beginningless beginning of time.

I soon began to realize that the whole message of the Buddha is directed to answering these fundamental questions about the self, this self bound by a karmic past and yearning for liberation and freedom.

centered around the different gods and goddesses. Smai Tawi are the yogic disciplines, techniques or technologies used to transform a human being. These disciplines promote a transformation through a movement that purifies the personality and renders it subtle enough to perceive the transcendental spiritual reality beyond time and space. This is a movement from ignorance to enlightenment, from mortality and weakness to immortality and supreme power, to discover the Absolute from whence the gods and goddesses and all Creation arose.

Yoga is the practice of mental, physical and spiritual disciplines which lead to self-control and self-discovery by purifying the mind, body and spirit, so as to discover the deeper spiritual essence which lies within every human being and object in the universe.

Enlightenment is the term used to describe the highest level of spiritual awakening. It means attaining such a level of spiritual awareness that one discovers the underlying unity of the entire universe as well as the fact that the source of all creation is the same source from which the innermost Self within every human heart arises.

All forms of spiritual practice are directed toward the goal of assisting every individual to discover the true essence of the universe both externally, in physical creation, and internally, within the human heart, as the very root of human consciousness. Thus, many terms are used to describe the attainment of the goal of spiritual knowledge and the eradication of spiritual ignorance. Some of these terms are: Enlightenment, Resurrection, Salvation, The Kingdom of Heaven, Moksha or Liberation, Buddha Consciousness, One With The Tao, Self-realization, to Know Thyself, etc.

The essence of Creation and therefore, of each individual human being, is transcendental; it transcends the ordinary bounds of mental perception and understanding. However, all human experiences occur in and through the mind. Therefore, the heart of all human experiences, be they pain or pleasure, is rooted in the mind, the psyche. The purpose of mythology is to bridge the gap between the limited human mind and that which transcends all.

The study of mythical stories is important in order to gain insight into the "Psycho-Mythology" or psychological implications of mythology for the psycho-spiritual transformation of the individual which leads to the attainment of Enlightenment.

Myths are symbols which speak to people in a psycho-symbolic way. This psychological language of myths can lead people to understand and experience the transcendental truths which cannot be easily expressed in words.
Behind each principle there are many implications which must be understood and practiced in daily life in order for the teachings to become an integral part of life.
Rituals are the medium through which the myths are practiced, lived and realized.

Thus, when you delve into a myth, you must expect more than just entertainment. You should be equipped with the knowledge which will allow you to decipher the hidden meanings in the story so that you may also begin to experience and benefit from them on a personal level. Only then will you be able to engender a real transformation in your life which will lead you to Enlightenment.

The first and most important key to understanding a mystical myth is comprehending that the myth is not talking about some ancient personality or story which occurred a long time ago and which has no relevance to the present. In fact, the myth is speaking about you. It is a story about human life, its origins, its destiny, its plight and the correct action for leading a truly successful life which paves the way to Enlightenment and true happiness.

The second key to understanding a mystical myth is comprehending that it is usually written in the form of a journey in which the subject must learn about himself/herself and transcend the ordinary human consciousness.

ultimately, to spiritual Enlightenment.        The third key to understanding a mystical myth comes from living the myth. Living a myth does not mean simply reading a myth, being able to recount the events with perfect memory or simply practicing the rituals of a myth without a deeper understanding of their implications and purpose. It means making the essence of the teaching being conveyed through the myth an integral part of your life. If this practice is not implemented, the teachings remain at the intellectual level and the deeper truths of the myth are not revealed. Therefore, you must resolve to discover the myth in every facet of your life, and in so doing, you will be triumphant as the hero(ine) of the myth.
